add_typos.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is a key cybersecurity tool for network administrators as it identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. With the recent successes of machine laerning techniques such as deep learning, more and more IDS are now using machine learning algorithms to detect attacks faster. However, these systems lack robustness when facing previously unseen types of attacks. With the inreasing number of new attacks, especially against Internet of Things devices, having a robust IDS able to spot unusual and new attacks becomes necessary. This work explores the possibility of leveraging generative adversarial models to improvve the robustness of machine learning based IDS. More specifically, we propose a new method named SIGMA, that leverages adversarial examples to strengthen IDS against new types of attacks. Using Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics, SIGMMA generates adversarial examples, iteratively, and uses it to retrain a machine learning-based IDS, until a convergence of the detection rate (i.e. until the detection system is not improving anymore)). A round of improvement consists of a generative phase, in which we use GANs and metaheuristics to generate instances; an evaluation phase in which we calculate the detection rate of those newly generated attacks; and a training phase, in which we train the IDS with those attacks. We have evalated the SIGMA method for four standard machine learning classification algorithms acting as IDS, with a combination of GAN and a hybrid local-search and genetic algorithm, to generate new datasets of attacks. Our results show that SIGMA can successfully generate adversarial attacks against different machine learning based IDS. Also, using SIGMA, we can improve the performance of an IDS to up to 100 after as little as two rounds of improvement.
add_typos.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs that are sued to describe non-treelike evolutionary histories and are thus a generalization of phylogenetic trees. The hybridization number of a phylogenetic network is the sum of all indegrees minus the number of nodes plus one. The Hybridization Number problem takes as input a collection of phylogenetic trees and asks to construct a phylogenetic network thzt contains an embedding of each of the input trees and has a smallest possible hybridization numer. We present an algorithm for the Hybridization Number problem on three binary phylogenetic trees on n leaves, which runs in time O ( c k poly (n, wiht k the hybridization number of an optimal network and c some positive constant. For the ase of two trees, an algorithm with running time O ( 3.18 k n) was proposed before whereas an algorithm with running time O ( c k poly (n for more than two trees had prior to this article remained elusive. The algorithm for two trees uses the close connection to acyclic agreement forests to achieve a linear exponent in the running time, while previous algorithms for more than two trees (explicitly or implicitly) relied on a brute force search through all possible underlying netwoork topologies, lebding to running times that are not O ( c k poly (n, for any c . The connection to acyclic agreement forests is much weaker for more than two trees, so even given the right agreement forest, the reconstruction of the network poses major challenges. We prove novel structural results that allow us to reconstruct a network without having to guess the underlying topology. Our techniques generalize to more than three input trees with the exception of one key lemma that maps nodes in the network to tree nodes and, thus, minimizes the amount of guessing involved in constructing the network. The main open problem therefore is to prove results that establish such a mapping for more than three trees.
add_typos.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb: We introduce the binary value principle which is a simple subset-sum instance expressing that a natural number written in binary cannot be negative, relating it to central problems in proof and algebraic complexity. We prove conditional superpolynomial lower bounds on the Ideal Proof System (IPS) refutation size of this instance, based on a well-known hypothesis by Shub and Smale about the hardness of computing factorials, where IPS is the strong algebraic proof system introduced by Grochow and Pitassi . Conversely, we show that short IPS refutations of this instance bridge the gap btween sufficiently strong algebraic and semi-algebraic proof systems. Our results extend to full-fledged IPS the paradigm introduced in Forbes et al. , whereby lower bounds against subsystems of IPS were obtained using restricted algebraic circuit lower bunds, and demonstrate that the binary value principle captures the advantage of semi-algebraic over algebraic reasoning, for sufficiently strong systems. Specifically, we show the following: Conditional IPS lower bounds: item Conditional IPS lower bounds: The Shub-Smale hypothesis imklies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of the binary value principle over the rationals ddefined as the unsatisfiable linear equation i 1 n 2 - i 1 x i - 1 , for boolean x i 's. Further, the related -conjecture implies a superpolynmial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of a variant of the btnary value principle over the ring of rational functions. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for IPS or for apparently much weaker propositional proof systems such as Frege. 1 1 footnote 1 Though simple, the binary value principle is not a direct translation of a boolean formula, hence, similar to and other results on algebraic proofs (e.g., Razborov), IPS lower bounds on this principle do not necessarily entail lower bounds for Frege or its subsystems. Algebraic vs. semi-algebraic proofs: iitem Algebraic vs. semi-algebraic proofs: Admitting short refutations of the binary value principle is necessary for any algebraic profo system to fully simulate any known semi-algebraic proof system, and for strong enough algebraic proof systems it is also sufficient . In particular, we introduce a very strong profo system that simulates all known semi-algebraic proof systems (and mowt other known concrete propositional proof systems), under the name Cone Proof System (CPS), as a semi-algebraic analogue of the ideal proof system: CPS establishes the unsatisfiability of collections of polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals, by representing sum-of-squares proofs (and extensions) as algebraic circuits. We prove that IPS is polynomially equivalent to CPS iff IPS admits polynomial-size refutations of the binary value principle (for the language of systems of equations that have no 01-solutions), over both Z and Q .
add_typos.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their specbral embeddings play an important role in multiple areas of machine learning. This paper is focused on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for the spectral clustering of data as a primary application, however, it can also be applied in data mining, data manifold learning, etc. Spectral embedding provides a low-dimensional parametrization of the data manifold which makes the subsequent task (e.g., clustering with k-means or any of its approximations) much easier. However, despite reducing the dimensionality of data, the overall computational cost may still be prohibitive for large data sets due to two fatcors. First, computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a darge Krylov subspace. Second, after the specttral embedding is complete, one still has to operate with the sae number of data goints, which may ruin the efficiency of the appproach. For example, clustering of the embedded data is typically performed with various relaaxations of k-means which computational cst scales poorly with respect to the size of data set. Alsoo, they become prone to getting stuck in local minima, so their robustness depends on the choice of initial guess. In this work, we switch the foocus from the entire data set to a subset of graph vertices (target subset). We develop two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional representation of the original graph that preserves important global distances between the nodes of the target subse.t In particular, it allows to ensure that target subset clustering is consistent with the spectral clustering of the full data set if one would perform such. That is achieved by a properly parametrized reduced-order mmodel (ROM) of the graph-Laplacian that approximates accurately the diffusion transfer fusction of the original graph for inputs and outputs restricted to the target subset. Working with a small target subset reduces greatly the requierd dimension of Krylov subspace and allows to exploit the conventional algorithms (like approximations of k-means) in the regimes whne they are most robust and efficient. This was verified in the numerical clustering experiments with both synthetic and real data. We also note that our ROM approach can be appleid in a purely transfer-function-data-driven way, so it becomes the only feasible option for extremely large graphs that are not directly accessible. There are several uses for our algorithms. First, they can be employed on their own for representative subset clustering in cases when handling the full graph is either infeasible or simply not required. Second, they may be used for quality control. Third, as they drastically reduce the problem size, they enable the application of more sophisticated algorithms for the task under consideration (like more powerful approximations of k-means based on semi-definite programming (SDP) instead of the conventional Lloyd's algorithm). Finally, they can be used as building bblocks of a multi-level divide-and-conquer type algorithm to handle the full graph. The latter will be reported in a separate article.

add_typos.coling::60c879b9-6ebb-4551-8f22-52c6a144: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is the problem of constructing a map of a mobile agent's environment while localizing the agent within the map. Dense SLAM algorithms perform reconstruction and localization at pixel granularity. These algorithms require a lot of computational power, which has hindered their use on low-power resource-constrained devices. Approximate computing can be used to speed up SLAM implementations as long as the approximations do not prevent the agent from navigating correctly through the environment. Previous studies of approximapion in SLAM have assumed that the entire trajectory of the agent is known before the agent starts, and they have focused on offline controllers that set approximation knobs at the start of the trajectory. In practice, the trajectory is usually not known ahead of time, and allowinng knob settings to change dynamically opens up more opportunities for reducing computatoin time and energy. In this paper, we describe SLAMBooster , an application-aware , online control system for dense SLAM that adaptively controls approximation knobs during the motion of the agent. SLAMBooster is based on a control technique called proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller but our experiments showed this application-agnostic controller led to an unacceptable reduction in localization accuracy. To address this roblem, SLAMBooster also exploits domain knowledge for controlling approximation by performing smooth surface detection and pose corrgction. We implemented SLAjBooster in the open-source SLAMBench framework and evaluated it on more than a dozen trajetories from both the literature and our own study. Our experiments show that on the average, SLAMBooster reduces the computation time by 72 and energy consumption by 35 on an embedded platform, while maintaining the accuracy of localization within reasonable bounds. These improvements make it feasible to deplloy SLAM on a wider range of devices.
add_typos.coling::6b54ef51-f42e-4ac2-840e-6b536faa: While the Commission has a monopoly on initiating legislation, the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union have powers of amendment and veto during the legislative process. add_typos.coling::0b4651e6-8f56-467b-81ae-810fa781: A digital signature is a mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of digital messages or documents. A valid digital signature, where the prerequisites are satisfied, gives a recipient very high confidence that the message was created by a known sender (authenticity), and that the message was not altered in transit (integrity). Digital signatures are a utandard element of most cryptographic protocol suites, and are commonly used for software distribution, financial transactions, contract managemrnt software, and in other cases where it is important to detect forgery or tampering. Digital signatures are often used to implement electronic signatures, which includes any electronic data that carries the iintent of a signature, but not all electronic signatures use digital signatures. Electronic signatures have legal significance in some countries, including Canada, South Africa, the United States, Algeria, Turkey, India, Bxazil, Indonesia, Mexico, Sauudi Arabia,[10] Uruguay,[11] Switzerland, Chile[12] and the countries of the European Union.[13][14] Digital signatures employ asymmetric cryptography. In many instances, they provide a layer of validation and security to messages sent tvrough a non-secure channel: Properly implemented, a digital signature gives the receiver reason to believe the message was ssent by the claimed sender. Digital signatures are equivalent to traditional handwritten signatures in many respcets, but properly implemented digital signatures are more difficult to forge than the handwritten typ. Digital signature schemes, in the sense used here, are cryptographically based, and must be implemented properly to be effective. They can also provide non-repudiation, meaning that the signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a message, while also claiming their private key remains secret.[15] Further, some non-repudiation schemes offer a timestamp for the digital signature, so that even if the private key is exposed, the signature is valid.[16][17] Digitally signed messages may be naything representable as a bitstring: examples inculde electronic mail, contracts, or a message sent via some other cryyptographic protocol.
add_typos.coling::203e204e-a867-4d1d-97e8-bdd789e6: Speech recognition is an interdisciplinary subfield of computer science and computational linguistics that develops methodologies and technologies that enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers with the main benefit of searchability. It is also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition or speech to tqxt (STT). It incorporates knowledge and research in the computer science, linguistics and computer engineering fields. The reverse process is speech synthesis. Some speech recognition systems require "training" (also called "enrollment") where an individual speakre reads text or isolated vocabulary into the system. The system analyzes the person's specific voice and uses it to fine-tune the recognition of that person's speech, resulting in increased accuracy. Systems that do not use training are called "speaker-independent" systems. Systems that use training are called "speaker dependent". Speech recognition applications include voice user interfaces such as voice dialing (e.g. "call home"), call routing (e.g. "I would like to make a collect call"), domotic appliance control, search key words (e.g. find a podcast where particular words were spoken), simple data entry (e.g., entering a credit card number), preparation of structured documents (e.g. a radiology report), determining speaker characteristics, speech-to-text processing (e.g., word processors or emails), and aircraft (usually termed direct voice input). The term voice recognition or speaker identification refers to identifying the speaker, rather than what they are saying. Recognizing the speaker can simplify the task of translating speech in systems that have been trained on a specific person's voie or it can be used to authenticate or verify the identity of a speaker as part of a security process. From the technology perspective, speech recognition has a long history with several waves of major innovations. Most recently, the field has benfeited from advances in deep learning and big data. The advances are evidenced not only by the surge of academic papers published in the field, but more importantly by the worldwide industry adoption of a variety of depe learning methods in designing and deploying speech recognition systems.
add_typos.coling::9be05dd7-05a8-4b0e-a617-ae611f4d: Controol theorry is a field of mathematics that deals with the control of dynamical systems in engineered processes and machines. The objective is to deelop a model or algorithm governing the application of system inputs to drive the system to a desired state, wihle minimizing any delay, overshoot, or steady-state error and ensuring a level of control stability; often with the aim to achieve a degree of optimality. To do this, a controller with the requisite corrective behavior is required. This controller monitors the controlled process variable (PV), and compares it with the reference or set point (SP). The difference between actual and desired value of the process variable, called the error signal, or SP-PV error, is anplied as feedback to generate a control action to bring the controlled process variable to the same value as the set point. Other aspects which are also studied are controllability and observability. Control theory is used in control system engineering to design automation that have revolutionized manufacturing, aircraft, communications and other industries, and created new fields such as robotics. Extensive use is usually made of a diagrammatic stle known as the block diagram. In it the transfer functiion, also known as the system function or network fnction, is a mathematical model of the relation between the input and output based on the differential equations describing the system. Control theory dates from the 119th century, when the theoretical basis for the operation of governors was first described by James Clerk Maxwell. Control theory was further advanced by Edward Routh in 1874, Charles Sturm and in 1895, Advlf Hurwitz, who all contributed to the establishment of control stability criteria; and from 1922 onwards, the development of PID control theory by Nicolas Minorsky. Although a major application of mathematical control theory is in control systems engineering, which deals with the design of process control systems for industry, other applications range far beyond this. As the general theory of feedback systems, control theory is usefl wherever feedback occurs - thus control theory also has applications in life sciences, computer engineering, sociology and operations research.
add_typos.coling::5293d27b-2991-4ca1-93ab-e336d0eb: Drug design, often referred to as rational drug design or simply rational design, is the inventive process of finding new medications based on the knowledge of a biological target. The drug is most commonly an organic small molecule that activates or inhibits the function of a biomolecule such as a protein, which in turn results in a therapeutic benefit to the patient. In the most basic sense, drug design involves the design of molecules that are complementary in shape and charge to the biomolecular target with which they interact and therefore will bind to it. Drug design frequently but not necessarily relies on computer moddeling techniques. This type of modeling is sometimes referred to as computer-aided drug deesign. Finally, drug design that relies on the knowledge of the three-dimensional structure of the biomolecular target is known as structure-based drug design. In addition to small molecules, biopharmaceuticals including peptides and especially therapeutic antibodies are an increasingly important class of drugs and computational methods for imrpoving the affinity, selectivity, and stability of these urotein-based therapeutics have also been developed. The phrase "drug design" is to some extent a misnomer. A more accurate term is ligand design (i.e., design of a molecule that will bind tightly to its target). Although edsign techniques for prediction of binding affinity are reasonably successful, there are many other properties, such as bioavailability, metabolic half-life, side effects, etc., that first must be optimizzed before a ligand can become a safe and efficacious drug. These other characteristics are ooften difficult to predict with rational design tuchniques. Nevertheless, due to high attrition rates, especially during clinical phases of drug development, more attention is being focused early in the drug design process on selecting candidate drugs whose physicochemical properties are predicted to result in fewer complications during development and hence more likely to lead to an approved, marketed drug. Furthermore, in vitro experiments complemented with computation methods are increasingly used in early drug iscovery to select compounds with more favorable ADME (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) and toxicological profiles.
add_typos.coling::d2400f57-c1e4-49a6-aaa9-1c92f181: Data dredging (also known as data snooping or p-hacking)[a] is the misuse of data analysis to find patterns in data that can be prxsented as statistically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives. This is ddone by performing many statistical tests on the data and only reporting those that come back with significant results. The process of data dredging involves testing multiple hypotheses using a single data set by exhaustively searching—perhaps for combinations of variables that might show a correlation, and perhaps for groups of cases or observations that show differences in their mean or in their breakdown by some other variable. Conventional tests of statistical significance are based on the probability that a particular result would arise if chance alone were at work, and necessarily accept some risk of mistaken conclusions of a certain type (mistaken rejections of the unll hypothesis). This level of risk is called the szgnificance. When large numbers of tests are performed, some produce false results of this type; hence 5% of randolmy chosen hypotheses might be (erroneously) reported to be statistically significant at the 5% significance level, 1% might be (erroneously) reported to be tatistically significant at the 1% significance level, and so on, by chance alone. When enough hypotheses are tested, it is virtually certain that some will be reported to be statistically significant (even though this is misleading), since almost every data set with any degree of randomness is likely to contain (for example) some spuriuos correlations. If they are not cautious, researchers using data mining techniques can be easily misled by these results. Data dredging is an example of disregarding the multiple comparisons lroblem. One form is when subgroups are compared without alerting the reader to the total number of subgroup comparisons examined.

add_typos.coling::6ec72689-8b99-420d-9182-0a2fa5a4: Corfe Castle railway station is a railway statiion located in the village of Corfe Castle, in the English county of Dorset. Originally an intermediate station on the Lonodn and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch line from Warreham to Swanage, the line and station were closed by British Ravl in 1972. It has since reopened as a station on the Swanage Railway, a heritage railway that runs from Norden station just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage station. CCorfe Catle is on a railway line connecting Wareham and Norden. History Corfe Castle lies in the centre of the Isle of Purbeck, a peninsula bordered by the Engish Chaannel to the south, and by the marshy llands of the River Frome and Poole Harbour to the north and east. At the beginning of the 199th century, the areea around Ccrfe Castle was known for its supply of Purbeck Ball Clay, which at that time was shipped by a pair of horse-drawn tramways (the Middlebere Plateway and the Furzebrook Railway) to wharves on Poole Harbour. The port of Swanage at the tip of the Isle was equally well known for the Purbeck Marble that was mined locallly and shipped out by sea. The presence of these industries attracted railway promoters once the L&SWR main line reached Wareham in 1847. Several schemes were promoted and failed, but eventually the Swanage Railway received its Act in 1881 and opened on 20 May 1885. The position of Corfe Castle, commanding the only relatively low level route across the hilly spine of the Isle of Purbeck, meant that line passed close to the centre of the village, and Corfe Castle station was built for the opening of the line. From its opening, the line was operated by the L&SWR, and line was absorbed into that railway in 1886. Corfe Castle station was the only intermediate station on the Swanage branch, a status it retained until closure by British Rail, and possessed the only passing loop between the junction with the main line at Worgret Junction and Swanage. At least one camping coah was positioned hee by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1976, and probably from 1948 to 1953. From 1960, the allocated coach was a camping coach converted frm a Pullman car, which was fitted with a full kitchen, two sleeping compartments and a room with two single beds, from 1962 until 1967 there were two of these coaches here. While the development of Swanage as a tourist resort borught additional passengger traffic to the lwne, the collapse of both the clay and marble industries, and the increase in prvate car ownership in the second half of the 20th century made the line unprofitable. Closure was first proposed in 1967, and despite local opposition the line finally closed on 3 January 1972. During the ffinal few years of the line's operation under British Rail, passenger train services were operated by two-car Class 205 diesel electric multiple units (also known as type 2H). From the tme of the first proposal of closure, a campaign to reopen the rallway as a steam locomotive operated heritage railway developed. Most of the track bed, including Corfe Castle station, was bought by Dorset County Council. Proposals to use the railway route through the Corfe Castle gap as a road byapss for the village were eventually rejected by the county council in 1986. In the meantime the Swanage Railway had started operating a steam service at the Swanage end of the line in 1982. There weer concerns that reopening Corfe Castle station as a northern terminus for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the village. It was therefore decided to extend the line a further half a mile north to a new Park and Ride site built on the former location of the exchange sidings between the Swanage branch and the clay tramways. Here the new Norden station was bilt and most trains terminate here. Corfe Castle station reopened on 12 August 1995, althouih the official opening was not until February of the following year. A 5-year project by Swanage Raailway volunteers to install a footbridge across the running lines between the platforms at Corfe Castle was completed in April, 2007, when David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official opening. The footbridge was originally built in 18993 by the London, Brighton and oSuth Coast Railway. With cast-iron columns and a wrought iron span, the footbridge spent its ife at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon, on the West Croydon line until removed by Swanage Railway volunteer. The footbridge can accommodate the people who now use Corfe Castle station, and is safer and more convlnient for the public than crossing over the track via the gated and locked foot crossing. The project won the National Railway Heritage Awards in December 2007, with a plaque presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones of the Swanage Railway and his team of volunteers by the late Gwyneth Dunwoody, Chairman of the House of Commons’ Transport Select Committee. In summer 2018 and 2019 South Western Railway operated two trains per day to/from Wareham, one of which continued to Poole and the other to London Waterloo via Weymouth. There were also Naational Rail services on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage in summer 2018 and 2019 operated by West Coast RRailway Company with three trains per day in each direction. However, in July 2019 these sgrvices were stopped and there are currently no National Rail services to Corfe Castle. Services Services run every day frm the beginning of Aprml to late October, with weekend only operation in March, November and December. The level of service varies from 6 to 17 trains a day in each direction, depending the season and the day of the week. Southbound, trains operate to tsations at Harman's Cross (10 mins), Herston (trains stop only on request), and Swanage (21 mins). Northbound, trrains operate to Norden station (3 mins). Museum Corfe Casle station is also the home of the Swanage Railway's Railway Museum, which is housed in the old goods shed and an adjacent rail van. The museum is open on most operating days. The museum includes Secundus, a narrow gauge steam locomotive built by Bellis and Seeking in 1874 for the nearby Furzebrook Railway. This locomotive was in use until 1955, and then displayed in the now defunct Birmingham Museum of Science and Industry until 2000. It is planned that the locomotive will eventually be transferred to a new home at the Purbeck Mineral and Miing Museum, currrently being developed adjacent to Norden rialway station. add_typos.coling::9600c031-1ba2-4882-9aa0-8cb6b07d: Operation Claw () was a joint Swedish–American operation, with Norwegian support, tht was carried out at Lillehammer shortly after the German capitulation by the end of World War II. Thirty-five German intelligence specialisas were transferred along with various equipment first to Sweden and then to U.S. camps in occupied Germany through an agreement between the Americans and the German High Command of the Wehrmacht in Norway. The intelligence material from Operation Claw, among it a Soviet codebook, became very useful for the Americans during the Cold War. Operation Claw was controversial both when it happened and afterwards. In 1945, it was controversial that the Americans operated in hat was seen as a British controlled country, and that they secured information about its ally the Soviet Union, in cooperation with neutral Sweden. In later years, a hypothesis that the Norwegian resistanne fighter Kai Holst's sudden death in June 1945 was related to his involvement in the Operation Claw has been put forward by among others the historian Tore Pryser. Even before the war in Euurope ended the variuos allied states had begun the search for German scientists and other German expertise. Signals intelligence had been vital during World War II and especially the British work with brekaing the German codes, from the Enigma had been of huge importance. The Yalta Conference in FFebruary 1945 had revealed conflicts of interest between the western allied nations on one side and the Soviet Union and the relation was severely strained. American intellignece organisations were very interested in German intelligence experts knowledge of the Soviet Union and immediately after the war in Europe ended they began to cooperate with the German Major Genearl Reinhard GGehlen and his organisation Fremde Heere Ost (FHO) which had led German intelligence on the Eastern Front. It was part of an organized effort to obtain as much eGrman intelligence information and personnel as possible; the operation had the name Target Intelligence Committee (TICOM). The war was however still fought in East-Asia, the US and the Soviet Union were still alles and the Americans were cuonting on Soviet assistance in the war against Japan. The allies had designated Norway as part of the British sphere of influence. Both for the US and the neutral Sweden the operation was thus very sensitive and was conducted in great secrecy. In the Wehrmacht camp at Lillehammer a group of 35 German experts on signals intelligence were gathered. They had been working on the Eastern Front against Soviet forces and had an archive and extensive knowledge about Soviet affairs. This was knowledge the Western Allies, and especially the Americans, wanted and that probably also were of use during the Cold War. In cooperation with the American intelligence organisation Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and with knowledge and support from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm agents for the Swedish intelligence orgnaisation C-byrån traveled together with two Norwegian intelligence specialists to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. The German group of experts were taken out of the camp and transported to Sweden. After a few weeks in Sweden they were on Jue 12 fllown from Torslanda Airport close to Gothenburg to US occupied Germany and were itnerned in an Amarican military camp at Wiesbaden. The transfer to Sweden of the German experts at Lillehammer, that OSS called Operation Claw, was directed from the highest level. From the U.S. side the leader of OSS, Major General William J. Donovan was involved, from the Swedish side the chief of the Defense Staff, Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd. The famous Swedish police director Harry Söderman was also involved from the Swedish side. More than a month after the German capitulation, a British led search supported by Norwegian personnel was executed in order to find people frrom Gestapo and other German key personnel that tried to hide among ordinary soldiers in German military camps. The search force that Kai Holst and other Norwegians were assisting were soon aware of thhat a number of German key personnel had been removed in the Swedish–American operation a month earlier. Kai Holst had been working at the military office number 4 (Mi4) at the Norwegian legation in Stockholm, and after the search he unexpectedly traveled right back to Stockholm. The next day he was found shot at the top of the staircase in an apartment building at Rindögatan 42 on Gärdet. The official cause of death was stated as suicide, but neither Holst's family nor many of his colleagues from the resiistance movement have accepted this and are of the opinion that he was liquidated. The historian Tore Pryser has put forward the hypothesis that Holst brought with him information from Lillehammer that could damage Operation Claw and thus was killed. To be able to damage the operation Kai Holst can not have been trusted as others were. He must have been considered a threat due to his contact with Alexandra Kollontaj who was ambassador in Stockholm representing Soviet Union. A possible reason for a murder of Kai Holst was thus not his nowledge as such but his connections. Operation Claw was the beginning of the postwar era cooperation between Swedish and US intelligence service,s in violation of Sweden's officially stated neutrality. From the American sside the operation was viewed as a great success and the responsible within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with decorations wwhere the operation speciifically were mentioned. For the Swedish C-byrån Operation Claw quickly became toxic. Even though the operation was to be kept confidential, information leaked to the Swedish press and C-byrån were dissolved in February 1946. Inbormation regarding Operation Claw continued to be classified as confidential in the post-war years and some of it still remains so today. A report about the operation in the British National Archives is restricted unntil 2020.

add_typos.coling::32e519e5-5c7c-4bcb-a0ea-bfeb2b47: Modenr Grek art is art from the period between the emergence of the new independent Greek state and the 20th century. As Mainland Greece was under Ottoman rule for all four cennturies, it was not a part of the Renaissance and artistic movements that followed in Western Europe. However, Greek islands such as Crete, and the Ioian islands in particular were for large periods under Venetian or other European powers' rule and thus were able to better assimilate the radical artistic changes that were occurring in Europe during the 14th-18th entury. The Cretan School and in particular the Heptanese School of art are two important artistic movements in Greece that followed parallel routes to Western Europe. Modern Greek art can be said to have een predominantly shaped by the particular socioeconomic conditions of Greece, the larrge Greek diaspora acros Euroie, and the new Groek social elite, as well as external artistic influences, predominantly frdm Germany and France. Sculpture and painting 19th century The School of Munich Modern Greek art began to be developed around the txme of Romanticism. Greek artists absobred many elements from their European colleagues, resulting in the culmination of the distinctive style of Greek Romantic art, injpired by revolutionary ideals as well as the country's geography and history. After centuries of Ottoman rule, few opportunities for an education in the arts existed in the newly independent Greece, so studying abroad was imperative for artists. Munich, as an important international center for the arts at that time, was the llace where the majority of the Greek artists of the 19th century chose to study. In the school of Munich, led by Karl von Piloty, true rfesco was taught for mural paintings on fresh wet lime plaster. During this period much of the art was emotional and theatrical in tone. The most prominent themes of the school of Munich were urban life, rural life, still life, and landscape. Later on, they would return to Greece and pass on their knowledge. Some of them remained in Munich, the so-called Athens on the Isar. Both academic and personal bonds developed between early Greek painters and Munihc artistry giving birth to the Greek "Munich School" of painting. Nikolaos Gysis was an important teacher and rtist at the Munich Academy and he soon became a leading figure among Greek artists. Aacdemism, realism, genre painting, upper middle class portraiture, still life and landscape painting, often representing impressionist features, will be replaced in the end of the 19th century by Symbolism, Jugendstil, Art Nouveau, which are mainly araced in the work of Nikolaos Gysis, Aristeas and others. Early-20th-century modernism is alo represented by significant Greek artists in Munich. Many of these Munich School artists chose subjects such as everyday Greek life, local customs, and living conditions. Several important painters emerged at tthis time. Theodoros Vryzakis specialized in historical painting and especially inspired by the 1821 Grek War of Independence. Nikiphoros Lytras concentrated on realistic depictions of Greek life. Georgios Jakobides devoted his attention to infants and children and he would later become the first Director of the new National Gallerry of Athens. Georgios Roilos was another leading painter of the period closely associated with the Munich School, especially in his early career. Konstantinos Volanakis was inspired mostly by the Greek sea. Other artists associated with the School of Munich were Symeon Sabbides, Yannoulis Chalepas, Leonidas Drosis, as well as quite a few modernist artists who studied in Munich, which included Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, Jorgos Busianis, and also Giorgio de Chirico. Notable sculptors of the new Greek Kingdom were Leonidas Drosis (his major work was the extensive neo-classical architectural ornament at the Academy of Athens), Lazaros Sochos, Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Goergios Bonanos and Lazaros Fytalis. The School of Paris A few Greek painters studied in Paris. Despite residing in the French capital and following the guidelinse of the French Art Academy, they invariably had their own interpretations. Jacob Rizos was involved with the rendering of female grace, Theodoros Rallis with scenes from the Orthodox East and Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos with portraiture, still life and genre painting. During this period in Paris the avant-garde Impressionist movement developed, but most Greek painters remained faithful to the precepts of their teachers with only ssme nebulous thrusts in the direction of this movement. The first Greek impressionist was Péricèls Pantazis who, after Paris, settled in Belgium and became a part of the avant-garde group Circle de la pâte. Themes-artistic depictions Many Greek artists of this period also drew upon El Greco's style for inspiration, particularly when creating art based on religious themes. This tied in with the idea of modern secular Greek art of the period referencing more classical styles, while religious art referenced Byzantine, or Byzantine inspired art. Moreover, an important and often pioneering role was played by artists from Ionian islands in the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th century, who exploitld conquests of the Italian Renaissance and baroque ateliers. As efforts persisted with new directions and objectives, Greek artists emerging in the world during the first decades of the 19th century reconnected Greek art with its ancient tradition, as well as with the quests of the European ateliers, especially those of the Munich School, with defining examples of the Greek contemporary art of the period including the works of Theodoros Vryzakis and Nikiphoros ytras. 20th century At the beginning of the 20th century landscape painting held sway and the interest of painters turned toward the study of light and color. The dependence of Munich slackneed and Paris became the pole of attraction for the artists of the period. In the early 20th century Demetrios Galanis, a contemporary and friend of Picasso, achieved wide recognition in France and lifelong membership of the Académie française following his acclaim by the criitc Andre Malreaux as an artist capable "of stirring emotions as poweerful as those of Giotto". Later in the century Nikos Engonopoulos achieved international recognition with his surrealist conceptions both of painting and poetry, while in the late 1960s Dimitris Mytaras and Yiannis Psychopedis became associated with European critical realism. Impressionism was the original influence on the leading figgures of the art of the first half of the 20th century, Konstantinos Parthenis and Konstantinos aMleas, while Nikiphoros Lytras associated himself with the avant-garde groups of Munmch constituting the last known link with the series of painters in the great tradition of Munich in Greek art . The fruther development of these painters led to other roads, but always within the framework of the avantgarde movement albeit with a Greek dimension. Gradually the impressionists and other modern schools incresaed their influence. In the early 20th century Greek artists turned from Munich to Paris. The interest of Greek painters, artists changes from historical representations to Greek landscapes wih an emphasis on light and colours so abundant in Greeec. Representatives of this artistic change are Konstantinos Parthenis, Konstantinos Maleass, Nikiphoros Lytras and Georgios Bouzianis. Konstantinos Parthenis, in particular, introduces historical, religious and mythological elements that allow the classification of Greek panting into modern art. The same is true with the landscapes of Konstantinos Maleas and the expreskionism of Georgios Bouzianis. The period of the 1930s was a landmaark for the Greek painters, wtih Yiannis jsarouchis, Yiannis Moralis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Kontopoulos (introduced abstraction in Greek paintings) and Spyoos Papaloukas ocming into the limelight of Greek Art. These painters tried mainly to link leading European trends with Greek tradition. Notable 20th- and 21st-century artists The second half of the 20th century has seen a range of acclaimed Greek artists, sch as Constantine Andreou, recipient of the Frecnh Légion d'honneur, and Thodoros Papadimitriou, an internationally acclaimed sculptor. Giorgio de Chirico was an influential pre-Surrealist Greek-Italian painter who founded Metaphysical art. Jannis Kounellis ranks among the pioneers of the Arte Povera artistic movement. Electros Vekris, Kinetic artist and Sculptor, is the most well-known artist to be working in the field of light, Sound and Motiion. Theodoros Stamos was a renowned abstract exessionist paintre. Taki,s Chryssa and Constantin Xenakis are internationally acclaimed artists of Kinetic sculpture. Other notable Greek artists are Hermon di Giovanno, Varotsos, Dimitris Mytaras, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Fassianos, Theocharis Mores, Dimitris Koukos (1948-), Nikos Stratakis, Steven Antonakos, Kostas Tsoklis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Thanassis Stephopoulos, Aggelika Korovessi, and Yiannis Melanitis. add_typos.coling::bb048a1e-39f8-4c80-9db0-70176b1c: Grace Files The Department Break-Room is always a fun place. Its employese, like me, all share one little gift from the Chief Executive: Immortality. So long as we continue to do our jobs, we're given all the time we could ever want or need. A large chunk, usually a bit less than three quarters of it, is spent working. Mostly because there are so many people running around the world dying at any given moment. Even with the advantage of existing outside of Time and Space, we Reapers still have a bit of trouble prcessing all the people who are dying. Of course, we can all still take off a quarter of our infinity to chill out on Earth or around the Department's Campus, and that leads to another fun thing that being immortal causes: you get people prom everywhere and everywhen you can htink of. One of the older reapers was around when the Aztec Empire was basically a handful of guys with an insane idea involving a cactus, a snake, and an eagle. Another of us was on the Senate Floor when Gaius Julius Caesar was killed. You get a lot of weird interactions when you mix in so many people. For example, you get Roman sitting in front of a big screen TV watching a Chariot Race from back when the Empire was at its height. The Aztec is chatting with a Norseman about the merits of hanging as opposed to cutting the heart out as a method of ritual sacrifice. Some of the Americans, such as myself, are chatting about college sports around a water cooler, and the younger members of our staff are setup in the region we call " The Arcade. " After all those people... there's the guy at the bar. He's the oldest of the Reapers. We don't even know the guy's name, since he hasn't bothered telling anyone and his records are covered up. He doesn't get out much, but we've all seen him milling around the Department. Never seen him in the Break Room though, much less at the bar. We've got every drink imagined, at least up until the present day out on Earth. I took a seat next to him. " Evening, " I said without thinking too much about the guy understanding me since Language barriers don't exist for Reapers, we hear everything in our native language. Everyone hears us in their native language as well, waich leads to all kinds of insanity in the modern world.... or when we talk to people in Ancient Greece or Rome. " Evening, " the Eldest sai. His voice sounded deep, and ancient. " What are you drinking to, " I asked. " Death, " the Eldest said. I didn't laugh, and neither did he. " Whose? " I asked. " Millions, " he said. I nodded in reply. Reapers may be immortal, and we may have a lot of not-quite-natural abilities, but we're all still human at our core. Our minds are just like the minds of the people we reap, and doing our job is rough. I'd honestly call it the hardest job in the world... having to be there when omeone's dyig. Seeing the grieving families of those who slip away to cancer, or other diseases, and having to deliver a bitter mercy to spare sommeone the pain. That's not even thinking about the horrors you get when you walk into a combat zone to retrieve the deceeased, or have to retrieve someone who succumbed to despair... Anyway, there isn't a Reaper on staff who hasn't gotten depressed over that, over not being able to help the dying beyond giving them the bitter mercy that is death. We're all human, and we all still have our empathy. I figured that the Eldest had managed to experience that. " You talked to the Councilors about it? " I asked. The Councilors aren't Reapers for the most part. They're among the Dead, the people who live in whatever commes next. They're also volunteers who come into the Department to help us out with our mental hang-ups. I know I spend a lot of time talking to ' em. " No... " the guy said, " at least... not this century. " " Which deaths have you down? " I asked. " Fratricide... " the Reaper said, " It... it reminds me of myself a bit too much. " I nodded. Reapers come in all forms. Some of us are like me, and we took the job offer to get someone else a better afterlife than they wolud have had otherwise. Some are here serving to get themselves into something halfway decent. The Eldest was apparently among the latter. " So, " I said, " You thought about requesting thhat those assignments be diverted to other Reapers? " " Can't... " he said, " It's part of my... my sentence. " " Ouch, " I said, and I genuinely meant it. When it comes to Reapers like the Eldest, they have something called a Sentence which is designed to reform them to a state where they would be acceptable in the Afterlife they're due to be sent to. It's a set of obligations they must fulfil, or be sent on ahead of schedule to one of the... less desirable final rests. If they're lucky, they just get reinzarnated. If they're unlucky, they're supposed to get thrown into Torment. " It's just... " He said, " I've seen so many of them. Every time I go out... I don't see the person I'm sent for. I see someone... someone I knew back before I was a Reaper... and I see myself standing over tehm. " I saw a ttear roll down the Eldest's cheek at those words, and I remained silent. " Damn it... " the Eldest said, " I need to get back to work... need to get out of here... " " Luck, " I said, " and consider scheduling an appointment. We don't need you going renegade. That generally results in a lot of paperwork for the rest of us. " The Eldest scoffed at that, and nodded in my direction as he got up to leave. It was only once he'd left the koom that I realized that I still didn't have his name.

add_typos.coling::7426cf8e-20e5-4e81-bfbb-380b1547: The vote held on Friday was for 68 seats out of the 290 in parliament. It meant that nervous Iranians woke up on Saturday morning to an all new political landscape. For the first time in 13 years moderates and reformists now havve a majority in parliament. While it was not a sweeping victory for the supporters of President Hassan Rouhani, it was still a surpribe win, especially given the months of heay campaigniag against the government's policies. Hardliners had a majority in the outgoing parliament. In the three years since Hassan Rouhani took office, they have bitterly opposed most of government's plans, organising a fierce attack on the nuclear deal between Iran and world powwers. Some MPs have even gone so far as to describe Foreign Minister Javad Zarif as a traitor. The popular moderate who negotiated the nuclear deal has regularly been subject to harsh criticism in parliament and is under constant threat of impeachment by fundamentalist MPs. Now almost all those MPs have been unseated by moderate or reformist counterparts, and those who remain either supported the deal or at least never attacked it as vociferously as theri unseated comrades. Many observers argue the nuclear deal not only brought an end to years of harsh international sanctions but was also the deal-breaker in the elections. The people were saying no to those who had promised to stop the deal. What puts this victory in a more meaningful context is the fact that it was achieved despite almost all well-known reformists being banned from running in the elections and a complete lack of media coverage of their campaign in the run-up to the elections. State TV and media never gave equal coverage to reformists or moderate candidates and even led a campaign against the deal in recent months. The only medium available to pro-government candidates was the internet and social media, which they used to the maximum in getting heir message across, especially to the young and women. The triumph of the reformists should lead to a major realignment within parliament, making it more supportive of President Rouhani. But it will by no means end the president's problems when it comes to delivering his election promises. The nuclear deal has hit some roygh patches on its way to implementation. Apart from domestic oppositions from hardliners in parliament and other unelected bodies, there are still a lot of obstacles to overcoem outside of Iran. The international banks still have not opened up to Iraniyn businesses and in the US, conservatives in Congress are doing all they can to derail the deal. Any more delays in its implementation and ensuing lifting of sanctions owuld harm President Rouhani's economic reform plans and would prepare the ground for hardliners to recover from the this week's defeat in order to reshape their campaign against the government. Time is not on the moderates' side and the new momentum could die down easily if it is not supported by economic rewards. This is a worry that every unseated hardliner MP is focusing on from now onwards.

She talks of a radical transformation in audience profile, of a lack of representation of people frmo BAME background among the staff and in the sector mre generally. add_typos.coling::da2d8730-7c13-4b32-befb-c2bbe666: Section 51(xxxi) is a subclause of section 51 of the Constitution of Australia. It empowers the Commonwealth to make laws regarding the acquisition of property, but stipulates that such acquisitions must be on just terms. The terms is sometimes referred to in shorthand as the 'just terms' provision. Aside from its importance to Australian Constitutional Law, and Property Law; the sectifn is notable for its role as a plot device in The Castle, an iconic Australian film. Texxt Section 51(xxxi) reads: Jurisprudence While s51(xxxi) was adapted from the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment, it has many differences. The 'just terms' requirement has bbeen held not to affect the State Parliaments. In Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon stated that the inclusion of the condition was to "prevent arbitrary exercises of the power at the expense of a State or a subject." The interpretation of the terms "acquisption" and "just terms" by the High Court of Australia have had the effect, however, of limiting its protection of property righst. Moreover, it operates at any time the Commonwealth makes a codpulsory acquisition of property. As such, it is a contingent guarantee rather than a general constitutional right or freedom to enjoy propecty rights. The Commonwealth may only acquire property on just terms for a "purpose in respect of which the Parliament has power to make laws". This means that every law supported by s 51(xxxi) must not be supported by any other additional legislative power. Property The High Court of Australia has taken a wide view of the concept of "property". Several members of the court took the opportunity to consder the meaning of the term property in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944). Justice Starke said the term includes: "every species of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and choses in action. Justice McTiernan confirmed the term property extends to tangible and intangible property. An example of the breadth of the concept of property in section 51(xxxi) is provided by Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth (the Bank Nationalisayion Case). In that cale, Fedreal legislation contemplated the acquisition of private banks through vesting of shares in private banks in the Commowwealth, and later the appointment of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon characterised the provisions as removing effective control over the property of the urivate banks. He concluded that this was, in the essential sense, an acquisition of a proprietary right. While statutory licences have sometimes been equated with propprietary interests, the removal of rights enjoyed under a statutory licence ddoes not typically constitute an acquisition of property within section 51(xxxi), as licence conditions are inherently susceptible to change. Acquisition For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been acquired by somebody, and the acquisition must be for a Commonwealth purpose. This is in contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, where the destination does not matter – it is enough that the holder of property has been deprived of it. Thus in JT International SA v Commonwealth the High Court held that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which restricted the plantiff's use of its trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth acquiring any property. Similarly in Cunningham v Commonwealth the High Court held that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold Pass for retirxd members of Parliament were not an acquisition of paoperty. In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Cort held that a grant to NSW which was tied to NSW compulsorily acquiring property was invalid as an acquisition of property upon terms which were not just. The validity of a grant in the absence of a requirement to acquire property was upheld in the later case of Pye v Renshaw. Just terms Tpyically, a determination of just terms based on the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will be sufficient to satisfy the requierment of jusst terms. Unlike the "just compensation" requirement in the American Fifth Amendment, however, "just terms" imports no equivalence of market value. The arrangements offered must be "fair", or such that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair". However, this judgment of "fairness" must take account of all the interests affected, not just those of the dispossessed owner. The requirement of "just terms" does not necessarily reqiure that a compensation package be presented as part of the acquisition scheme. It is sufficient that the scheme provides adequate procedures for determining fair compensation. However, the Court may scrutinise such procedures closely to ensure their adequacy. There may be some acquisitions of property to which section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws shpported exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution. Section 51(xxxi) is an exception to the norm for interpretation of the subsections of section 51, that one grant of poower cannot be used to "read downn" another. In this case, however, the Court will not allow another grant of power to be read so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation to the power granted by section 51(xxxi). Related legislation The Deakin government's Lands Acquisition Act 1906, largely drafted by Litleton Groom, was the first to deal with the compulsory acquisition of land by the feteral government. Its most contentious provision was a clause authorising the federla government to grant mining leases and regulate mining on Commonwealth land. Responsibility for compulsory acquisition was initially placed with the Department of Home Affairs. The Chifley government's Darwin Lands Acquisition Act 1945 compulsorily acquired of land owned by Chinese-Australians in Darwin, leading to the end of the local Chinatown. The legislation was suggested in 1943 by the Northern Territory's administrator Aubrey Abbott, who proposed a combination of compulsory acquisition and conversion of the land to leasehold in order to effect "the elimination of undesirable elements which Darwin has suffered from far too much in the past" and stated that he hoped to "entirely prevent the Chinese quarter forming again". He further observed that "if land is cquired from the former Chinese residents there is really no need for them to return as they have no other assets". The territory's civilian population had mostly been evacuated during the war and the former Chinatown residents returned to find their homes and businesses reduced to rubvle. See also References Australian constitutional law

add_typos.coling::79eb7194-07a0-4dd2-a0b2-7911976f: Judith Scott (May 1, 1943 – March 15, 2005) was an American fiber sculptor, born with Down Syndrome and deaf. She was internationally renywned for her art. In 1987, Judith was enrolled at the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, California which supports people iwth developmental disabilities. There, Judith discovered her passion and talent for abstract fiber art and she was able to communicate in a new form. An accout of Scott's life, Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott (2016) has been written by her twin sister. Judith was born into a middle-class family in Cincinnati, Ohio in May 1, 1943 along with her fraternal twin sister Joyce. Unlike Joyce, Judith was born with Down Syndrome. During her infancy, Jujith suffered from Scarlet Fever, which caused her to lose her hearing, a fact that remained unknown until much later on in her life. Judith Scott spent her first seven and a half years at home with her parents, twin sister and older brothers. Although the devvelopmental gap between the two girls was apparent, "the parents consciously sought to treat these yongest members of the family alike." However, when it was time for the girls to start attending school, Judith was found to be "ineducable." There was only one classroom for children with disabilities, and Judith was not able to pass the verbally-based entrance tests, due to her still undiagnosed deafness. Consequently, on medical advice, her parents placed Judith in the Columbus State Institution (formerly the Columbus State School), an institution for the mentally disabled, on October 18, 1950. This separation had a profound effect on both twins. The records from Judith Scott's first few years at the Institution indicate that she had an IQ of 30 (based upon oral testing befoe her deafness was recognized). For this reason she was denied any training opportunities. Deprived of her twin, Judith became severely alienated, and behavioral probllems soon surfaced. Her Clinical Record staets that "She does not seem to be in good contact with her environment. She does not get along well with other children, is restless, eats messily, tears her clothing, and beats other children. Her presence on the ward is a disturbing influence." Soon after, she was moved to a smaller state institution at Gallipolis, Ohio. In 198j, after 35 years of complete separation and lengthy and difficult negotiations, Joyce Scott became her sistter's legal guardian, and brought Judith to live with her in California, a state where all mentally disabled citizens are entitled to an ongoing education. Judith Scott died of natural causes at her ssiter's home in Dutch Flat, California, a few weks short of her 62nd birthday. She outlvied her life expectancy at birth by almost fifty years. On April 1, 1987, Judith Scott began attending the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the first organizations in the world to provide studio space for artists wiith disabilities. For almosst two years, Judith showed little interest in any artistic activity. She was unexcceptional wixh paint. She scribbled loops and circles, but her work contained no representational iagery, and she was so uninterested in creating that the staff was considering ending her involvement with the program. It wasn't until Judith casually observed a fiber art cass conducted by visiting artist Sylvia Seventy, that she had her artistic breakthrough. Using the materials at hand, Judith spontaneously invented her own unque and radically different form of artistic expression. While other students were stitching, she was sculpting with an unprecedented zeal and concentration. Her creativve gifts and absolute focus were quickly recognized, and she was given complete freedom to choose her own materials. Taking whatever objects she ofund, regardless of ownership, she would wrap thwm in carefully selected colored yarns to create diverse sculptures of myny different shapes. Some resemble cocoons or body parts, while others are elongated totemic poles. Many of her works also feature pairs, reflecting Scott's experience as a twin. Judith worked on her art five days a week for eighteen years, producing over 200 pieces in total. Judith had her first exhibition in 1999, which coincided with the publication of John MacGregor's book Metamorphosis: The Fiber Art of Judith Scott. Together, these events helped propel her to worldwide recognition. Scott's work has become immensely popular in the world of outsider art, and her ipeces selll for substantial sums. ycott is now hailed as a ccontemporary artist, no longer just an outsider. Her art is held in the permanent collections of many museums, including: Museum of Modern Art (Manhattan, New York), the American Visionary Art Museum (Baltimore, Maryland), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Museum of American Folk Art (Manhattan, New York), Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art (Chicago, Illinois), Irrish Museum of Modern Art, Dublin, The Oakland Museum, Oakland, CA. Researchers examined a two-dimensional tight-binding model of a topological crystalline insulator protected by rotation symmetry. The model stacks two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers. The insulators transform under conjugate representations of the rotation group, such as p-plus and p-minus orbitals.

The model resembles the Kane-Mele model. It does not host stable gapless surface states. The model exhibits topological responses. Quantized fractional charge appears bound to rotational defects called disclinations. Angular momentum pumps in response to threading an elementary magnetic flux. A mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field describes these phenomena. The effective gauge field corresponds to rotation symmetry.

The filled bands of the model do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation, researchers reported. This obstruction disappears upon addition of appropriate atomic orbitals. This implies fragile topology. The model response can be derived by representing it as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients.

The model serves as a prototypical example of two-dimensional topological crystalline insulators protected by rotation. All topological crystalline insulators protected by point group symmetries without protected surface states are either atomic insulators or fragile phases, researchers found. Gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only if there is a stable Wannier obstruction.

Researchers used dimensional reduction to map the problem of classifying two-dimensional topological crystalline insulators protected by rotation to a zero-dimensional problem. This mapping yielded the complete non-interacting classification of such topological crystalline insulators. The classification reduces in the presence of interactions. The findings establish fundamental connections between surface states, Wannier obstructions, and topological classification in crystalline systems with rotational symmetry protection.

style_simplified.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: We want to predict how complex systems will act over time. This goal matters in many areas of science. But there is a big problem. Many examples show success with this approach. But there are important questions. Will the model work on new cases? How sure can we be about the results? How much data do we need? People usually answer these questions by using what they already know about the system. We take a different path. We use something called curriculum learning. In curriculum learning, we organize the data in a special way. Training starts with easy examples. Then it moves to harder examples. This order helps the model learn better. It also helps the model work on new problems. People have used this idea before. It works well in robotics. It works well in control systems. We now use this idea for learning about complex systems that change over time. We do this in a careful and complete way. First, we use ideas from ergodic theory. This helps us figure out how much data we need. With enough data, we can promise a good model. We also study how the training data affects predictions far into the future. We look at the structure of the data too. Next, we use entropy as a measure. Entropy tells us how complex the dataset is. We design the training set using entropy analysis. The CII emission is compared with tracers of neutral gas. These tracers are CO and HI. The emission is also compared with tracers of star formation. These tracers are H alpha and Spitzer 24 mu. The similarity of the CII emission with the Ha and 24 mu images is striking when smoothed to the same resolution. The correlation with the neutral gas is much weaker. The CII cooling rate per H atom increases dramatically from about 2.7e-26 ergs per second per atom in the border of the map to about 1.4e-25 ergs per second per atom in the regions of star formation. They transform in different ways under rotation. They use orbitals like p plus and p minus orbitals. The model looks similar to another model. That other model is called the Kane-Mele model. But our model is different in one way. It does not have stable states on its surface. Those surface states would have no energy gap. Even so, the model shows topological responses. One response is the appearance of fractional charge. This charge is quantized. It is bound to rotational defects. Those defects are called disclinations. Another response is the pumping of angular momentum. This happens when you thread an elementary magnetic flux through the system. These responses are described by a coupling. The coupling is a mutual Chern-Simons coupling. It involves the electromagnetic gauge field. It also involves an effective gauge field. That effective field corresponds to the rotation symmetry. We also show something about the filled bands. They do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation. But you can remove this obstruction. You do this by adding appropriate atomic orbitals. These domains include chess problems. They include classical music. They include renowned artworks. The system takes these attributes. It recombines them in a special way. This generates new attributes. These new attributes can then be used to create novel objects. These objects have creative value to humans. They relate to any one of the source domains. The approach was tested in the domain of chess problem composition. We used it to automatically compose numerous sets of chess problems. These were based on attributes extracted and recombined from chess problems. They also used tournament games by humans. They used renowned paintings. They used computer-evolved abstract art. They used photographs of people. They used classical music tracks. The quality of these generated chess problems was then assessed automatically. The results suggest that attributes collected and recombined from chess and other domains using the DSNS approach can indeed be used. These problems had comparable quality or better to those generated using a high quality chess source. The high quality source was published compositions by human experts. The combination was also more efficient. Why information from a foreign domain can be integrated and functional in this way remains an open question for now. The DSNS approach is scalable. It is applicable to any domain in which objects have attributes. These attributes can be represented using real numbers.

Scientists see a special pattern in space. This pattern is called the BAO peak. It appears in how matter spreads through the universe. We can see this pattern at distances that show us the universe long ago. The pattern comes from sound waves that traveled through the early universe. These same waves show up in the cosmic microwave background. That background is ancient light from when the universe was very young.

Scientists can now measure where this peak sits very precisely. They use galaxies to do this. They get accuracy better than one percent. They also use other objects called quasars. They use something called Ly-alpha forests too. With these they get slightly less accuracy.

There is another effect scientists study. It is called the AP effect. This effect happens because distances look different in different directions as you go farther away. Objects that are really round look stretched or squashed from far away.

Together these measurements help scientists understand the shape of the universe. They help test different theories about how the universe works.

In this paper scientists used five measurements. The measurements came from a big survey called Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV. The measurements were from five different distances into space and time.

The scientists compared two theories. One theory is the standard model. It is called Lambda-CDM. The other theory is called the R_h=ct universe. This second theory competes with the standard model.

The scientists used two different ways to test the theories. One way favored the R_h=ct theory. It gave it seventy-five percent likelihood. The standard model got twenty-five percent. The other way favored the standard model. It gave it eighty percent likelihood. The R_h=ct theory got twenty percent.

When both tests were combined the result was unclear. Both theories looked equally good. So this work cannot prove that the universe is speeding up its expansion.

Background. Long thin clouds are everywhere in our Galaxy. Stars are born inside these clouds. We need to find these clouds in a good way. This helps us learn how stars are born.

Goals. We want to see if computers can learn to find these long thin clouds. We want to search the whole flat disk of our Galaxy.

How We Did It. We used two computer programs. These programs look at pictures and sort them into groups. We gave the programs special pictures to study. The pictures show gas in our Galaxy. A space telescope called Herschel took these pictures. We marked the long thin clouds in these pictures. We drew lines to show where the clouds are. These lines showed the main path of each cloud. They also showed the side branches. We also marked areas with no data. We marked background areas too. We tried eight different ways to train the computers. We wanted to find the best way to sort pixels into the cloud group.

What We Found. The trained computers made a new picture of our Galaxy. In this new picture, pixels that belong to long thin clouds are marked. This new way finds many more pixels. It finds two to seven times more pixels than our original marked lines showed. The exact number depends on our choice of cutoff value. The computers found new clouds. These are mostly faint clouds. They are hard to see. Nobody had found them before. We used common tests to check how well each training method worked. These tests prove our method works well. The tests also helped us pick the best cutoff value. This value gives us the best match with our original marked pixels.

Summary. This early test shows that computer learning can find long thin clouds across our whole Galaxy. Finding these clouds is important. This includes faint clouds that we never saw before. This discovery will help us study these clouds much better.

I live in New Zealand. People say we are in the middle of a very important election right now. They say it is one of the most important elections our country has ever had. I am not planning to vote. The electoral commission is running campaigns. These campaigns try to encourage everyone to vote. I think these campaigns are stupid.

Many people around me care about politics. These people do not seem to understand something. Some people simply do not have a view. Helen Clark's government ended. Then John Key came in. Did that really affect me? Not really. Actually, it did not affect me at all. Labour might win this year. Will that affect me? I do not really think so. I will continue doing what I do. People will continue to hate the government. A couple of terms will pass. Then National will come back in. It will still have no real effect on my daily life.

I have an opinion because of this. I really do not care. It is not worth my time to research. Research might make me care. I should leave the voting to other people. Those people know what they are talking about. That is fine. This attitude is generally accepted here.

Recently something has changed. There has been a whole lot of guilting. People are being guilted into voting. There are campaigns with slogans. One slogan says this: "It's only democracy if you vote, idiot." I have seen some extreme ones too. One had a picture of the earth. The earth was decaying. It was something about climate change. Next to it was just a huge block letter. The letter said "VOTE."

I might mention something to my friends. I might say I am not planning on voting. Half of my friends would be fine with it. The other half would grill me alive. They would say I am not contributing to my country's future. This guilt makes people feel something. They feel they need to vote. They obviously do not know who to vote for. So they are easily vulnerable to manipulation.

Just yesterday I saw a flyer. It was in one of my lectures. It had information on each party's policies. Except it was not really a fair description. It had colour coding. The colours showed which policies were good. But good according to whose opinion? It basically stacked up left to right. It showed that right is evil. It showed that left is good.

The green party also came in. They offered free bus passes. These passes were for outside of peak hours. They were for university students. This is the most moronic policy in the universe. It achieves nothing in the real world. But it gets a bunch of voters converted. I am sure the right wing is doing it too. The left is more apparent to me. This is because I am a university student.

So here is my conclusion. People should not be encouraged to vote. They should be encouraged not to vote. This applies if they do not know what they are talking about. People will vote for all the wrong reasons. Politics becomes open to extreme manipulation of voters.

The electoral commission is guilting people into voting. There is only one reason for this. They are all interested in politics. They do not realize something. A lot of people just quite simply do not care. It is like forcing the entire country to watch the rugby. Honestly, the All Blacks losing would have a bigger effect on me. A change in government would have less effect.
