style_simplified.coling::17ad7e76-2fa1-4c9b-a42b-44a53287: I am not sure what I think about this issue. But I will start by arguing against gay marriage. I have two reasons for this. First, I lean less toward the side I am starting with. That side seems much more fragile. That side is also less popular. Arguing for a weaker position helps me practice. It helps me get better at making arguments. I feel less strongly about this position. Second, I believe one side has the burden of proof. The side that favors gay marriage has that burden. I will explain why. Please watch this video. The video is only two minutes long. The video makes an argument. Because of that argument, I feel one side must prove its case. Some people want to redefine marriage. Those people want to change what marriage means. They must prove why we should change it. I do not have problems with changing definitions. But changing a definition requires a good reason. You need a compelling reason. People sometimes answer a question. The question is this: "Do you think gay marriage is a good idea?" They answer by saying "Why not?" This answer is a fallacy. It is called the teapot fallacy. They are trying to shift the burden of proof. That is not fair. I do not believe equality is a good argument here. People with different sexual orientations deserve equal rights. They deserve the right to life. They deserve liberty. They deserve freedom. They deserve the pursuit of happiness. The constitution details these rights. However, the equality argument is a red herring in this case. A red herring means it distracts from the real issue. Marriage is not a privilege. Marriage is not a right that must be equal for all types of relationships. Marriage is an institution. It was built around having children. It was built around procreation. Homosexual relationships may be loving. They may be committed. But by definition they cannot produce children. They are non-procreational. Some heterosexual marriages also cannot produce children. Old couples cannot have children. Infertile couples cannot have children. But if you watched the video, you will understand something. These cases are not the same. Just because there are exceptions does not mean you can extend the definition. The exceptions do not define the norm. The norm is not defined by its exceptions. This equality issue is not the same as women voting. It is not the same as black people being free. People often present criteria as a question. The question is this: "If two people love each other, why shouldn't they be able to get married?" Marriage criteria have nothing to do with love. They have nothing to do with romantic love either. If your criteria are two individuals who have romantic love, then incest is fair game. If your criteria are two individuals who have sexual love, then incest is also fair game. Some will argue that incest is different. They say there are power issues within the family. They say there are genetic defects. But there can be power issues within any relationship. Power issues can happen in heterosexual relationships. They can happen in homosexual relationships. They can happen in incestuous relationships. There is no reason to base marriage laws on this. Also, incestuous couples do not have to have children. They can adopt children. They may be infertile. They may be homosexual. One may argue that incest should be a valid form of marriage. One may argue it should be valid just like homosexuality. You can try to argue this point if you want. But please include valid reasoning. The burden of proof is on you. The argument "why would you care?" is invalid. Just because something does not affect anyone badly does not mean we can change institutions at whim. We cannot change things whenever we want. Even under utilitarianism, this argument does not work. Gay people can have fulfilling relationships. These can be long-term relationships. They can be romantic relationships. They can be sexual relationships. They do not need to call it marriage. Redefining marriage for the happiness of a group is similar to something else. It is like giving in to lobbyist demands. We give in so they will be happier. This is similar logically. It is not similar emotionally. Most arguments for gay marriage are appeals to emotion. They are appeals to popularity. The term "gay rights" was designed to make it sound like we have camps for them. Like we have internment camps. Even the term "homophobe" was created to stigmatize the opposition. This issue is popular in our time. Many opponents are religious fundamentalists. They use bad arguments. They use straw man arguments. But that does not make the other side correct. It does not make the "more reasonable side" right. Imagine a movement to legalize incestuous marriage. Imagine it was popular. There would be videos online. There would be websites online. They would glorify the struggle of such couples. Most people would be for that as well. Why is one sexual deviation more acceptable for marriage than another? I mean to use that term with complete respect. I mean absolutely no stigma. I mean no negative connotation. I mean no negative implication. My view changed. In all fairness, I was already seventy-five percent there when I wrote this.

These are two different questions. Let me explain.

Bridge: The Atlantic Ocean is very big. It is really really big. The size depends on where you cross. It can be bigger than the whole USA. The ocean is wet. It gets storms. Water and storms can damage concrete. They can damage steel too. You would need concrete and steel to build a bridge. The ocean is too deep. You cannot sink poles down to the bottom. The poles would hold up the bridge. But they cannot reach that far down. The ocean has many storms. It has big waves. You could try a floating bridge instead. That is called a pontoon bridge. But the waves would shake it. The bridge would break into pieces. The ocean is big. The ocean is empty. Not many people would want to drive across it. The drive would be very boring. Cars need fuel. They could not carry enough fuel for the whole trip.

Here is more detail. We cannot sink poles to hold the bridge steady. The materials we have cannot handle a floating bridge. The stress would be too much. Salt water causes rust. The air near the ocean also causes rust. Fixing the bridge would be very hard. You would need fuel on the crossing. Someone would have to ship fuel to the middle of the ocean. That does not make sense.

Tunnel: The Atlantic is very deep. There is lots of water above the ocean floor. All that water creates pressure. It pushes down on the bottom. Think about diving in a pool. Your ears hurt when you go deep. Now multiply that feeling by ten thousand times. That is how much pressure exists down there. They could try to dig a tunnel. But the tunnel could never spring a leak. Not even a tiny leak. If it did leak, the walls would fall down. Everyone inside would drown. You would need big fans. Very big fans. The fans would move air through the tunnel. Everyone needs air to breathe. You would have the fuel problem again too.

Here is more detail. The real problem is the joints. Workers would make tunnel sections ahead of time. Then they would put the sections into place. The sections would connect together. But the joints where they connect would not be strong enough. The pressure is too great. Even small leaks would be dangerous. Water under that much pressure cuts like a laser. It cuts like a laser in movies. Ventilation is another huge problem. The tunnel would be thousands of miles long. The air inside would be dead air. It would not move. You would need to circulate it somehow. Otherwise you could not make it through alive. Fuel is a problem here as well.

No, it cannot be done. The ocean is too big. It is too deep. It is too rough.

Someone found information about this idea. Is the tunnel possible? Maybe it is possible. Early engineers in the eighteen hundreds thought about space travel. They thought it might be possible someday. If enough scientists want this tunnel, it might get built. If enough politicians want it, it might get built. They would have to really want it. Otherwise, it will not happen.

Ask yourself some questions. Why would anyone want to drive across the Atlantic? What good would a bridge or tunnel do? Who would pay to build it? How would they get their money back? Who would take care of it after it was built? It would be in international waters. No country owns international waters. What country would be responsible? What local government would handle it? Who would manage the utilities? Who would manage the infrastructure? It is not realistic. It is not practical. It is not needed.

Tunnel: Here is another point. Most people have not mentioned this point. But it is important. The Mid Atlantic Ridge runs through the ocean. The Atlantic Ocean is pulling itself apart. It pulls apart at a rate of two and a half centimeters each year. You would have to deal with volcanoes. You would have to deal with earthquakes. Look at a map of the ocean floor. You can see what it looks like without water.

Even if someone builds a tunnel, would it be useful? Think about your car. How far can it travel before it needs more fuel? How many hours can you drive before you get too tired? What if something bad happens in the middle of the tunnel? Emergency workers would be hours away. It would take hours for them to reach you.

Yes, it is possible. We have the technology now. But it is not economically viable. The cost would be extremely high. The benefit would be very small. The project might become more realistic in the future. Technology will improve over the coming decades.

Sometimes there are not many athletes in one category. There are not enough athletes to fill up a whole race. When this happens, they run similar categories together. Athletes with less affected cerebral palsy can ride with athletes who have amputations that affect them less. But they are only scored in their own class. They do this at most bike races. It speeds things up. It consolidates the races.

The Paralympics have a complicated system. They use classifications and adjustments. They try to keep things as fair as possible. There are not a lot of disabled athletes. There is a wide variety of disabilities. Different disabilities give different advantages and disadvantages. For example, look at wheelchair sports. Amputees often have an advantage over people who are paralyzed. Amputees are lighter. Amputees are more able to move around. Sometimes they need to have enough people to hold a competition. They have to accept that some disability types will have an advantage. This is not really different from the regular Olympics. Tall people have an advantage in basketball. No one is trying to fix that.

The categories are based on what the disability causes. They are not based on the type of disability. Look at cycling. One category is for people with upper body disabilities. Another category is for people with one limb disability who can pedal with both legs. Another category is for people with a leg injury who only pedal with one leg. The last category is for people with both legs affected. If cerebral palsy affects the legs of an athlete, they would be put in the last category. Someone else with another disability that affects both legs would go there too. The athletes must be classified internationally. This requires an examination. The examination shows how the disability affects the athlete. This helps ensure that people cannot game the system. People cannot get placed in a category for more disabled athletes.

Some animals do not just play dead. They also make bad smells. The bad smells make predators think the meat has gone rotten. Not all predators can eat rotten meat. The predator will leave the animal alone. The predator will look for safer food instead.

Many predators cannot understand tricks. They do not think about whether something might be fooling them.

Animals that seem sick get avoided by predators. This makes sense. A sick animal might make the predator sick too. The sickness could even kill the predator. Playing dead might look simple. But the predator must think about risks. The predator worries about bacteria. The predator worries about viruses. The predator worries about other bad things.

Think about defending yourself from an attacker. Your body fills with adrenaline. You fight back very hard. You act crazy to protect yourself. Then the attacker stops moving. The danger seems over now. You start to feel safe again. It does not matter why they stopped. Maybe they are unconscious. Maybe they are dead. Maybe they are faking. You still feel safer. And you are a human. You can think and reason. Animals just follow instinct.

Prey animals have instincts to protect themselves. They trample attackers. They headbutt attackers. They bite attackers. They use horns to gore attackers. They use antlers to gore attackers. But once the threat stops moving, the instinct goes away. The prey animal loses interest.

Hunting animals work the same way. They see prey running away. They see prey moving around. This triggers their aggression. The movement makes them want to attack. When the prey stops moving, they lose interest. They only care about feeding if they feel hungry.

Take a bear as an example. A bear shows territorial aggression. A bear shows defensive aggression. The bear loses interest when the crisis ends. Playing dead works on a bear.

But this trick does not work on all predators. Think about a pack of wolves. Wolves want to eat you. When you stop struggling, they think dinner is ready. They start eating right away.

The reason is the camera's field of view. People call this FOV. Some people play first person shooter games. Those people know about FOV. Some people know about cameras. Those people also know about FOV. Think about what you can see. It starts at your eye. It goes out in a cone shape. You can see a picture of this at URL0. FOV is an angle. It is the angle between the two sides of the cone. Players in shooter games often make the FOV bigger. This gives them an advantage. They can see more around them. There is an example at URL1. I found it on the internet. It shows what happens when you increase FOV in a game. The left image has FOV expanded to sixty five degrees. The default is forty five degrees. That is on the right. The larger FOV lets you see more. You see more on the left side. You see more on the right side. But notice something else. The two trailer things look farther away. The player is standing in the same place. This happens because you increased the FOV. The light from distant objects changes. It converges on your flat surface differently. A larger FOV makes objects shrink faster. They shrink as they get farther away. The opposite is also true. You can decrease the FOV. Then far away objects look bigger. They converge on a larger part of the view area. The camera on DSCOVR has a very small FOV. It is only zero point six one degrees. This makes it very good at collecting light from far away objects. It focuses on a very small cone. The distance between Earth and Moon matters less with this camera. It does not affect their relative size the same way. Regular cameras show size differently. Human eyes also show size differently.

Now hold your hand in front of your face. It is probably about as big as your monitor. Keep your hand in the same spot. Move your head backwards. Your hand now looks smaller than the monitor. There is a certain distance where things change. Your hand gets smaller. The monitor gets smaller. They get smaller together. They shrink at the same rate. This happens for a reason. The distance between you and those two things becomes much greater. It is much greater than the distance between those two things. Angular diameter depends on distance. It also depends on ratio of distances. The first image is very close to the moon. It is far from the earth. So the moon seems big. The second image is very far from both. It is far from the earth. It is far from the moon. So they appear like their actual relative sizes. The earth does appear smaller in the second image. But the moon got smaller much faster. It is just like your hand.

DSCOVR had its camera zoomed in more. The camera is called EPIC. It is on the spacecraft. It took the image. It is designed to observe Earth from a distance. The cameras on Apollo missions were different. They were more general purpose. In a camera the focal length matters. The focal length of the lens determines something. It determines the physical size of the image. The image forms on the sensor. The physical size of the sensor determines the field of view. The pixel resolution of the sensor also matters. It determines the size of each pixel in the image. Analogue film works differently. It has no pixels. But the film still has a resolution limit. This comes from its chemistry. The lens also imposes a resolution limit. Finally you can crop a large image. The DSCOVR image was not cropped much. It is pretty much its full size.
style_simplified.coling::1770be09-c92d-43e3-ab15-7b7318ca: You need to know that many types of radiation exist. Light is one type of radiation. You are asking about ionizing radiation. This is the type used in bombs. This is the type used in power plants. You need to know what an atom is first. An atom is a basic building block. Everything in the world is made of atoms. Atoms contain protons. Atoms contain neutrons. Atoms contain electrons. Different numbers of these parts make different atoms. Different combinations of these parts make different atoms. Most atoms are stable. Stable atoms do not change. Some atoms are not stable. The unstable ones want to become stable. They get rid of protons to become stable. They get rid of neutrons to become stable. They get rid of electrons to become stable. This happens over time. These parts are sent away very fast. The fast speed makes them dangerous. They are like tiny bullets. They hit other things at the atomic level. They can collide with another atom. They hit it with great force. That atom's protons scatter. That atom's neutrons scatter. That atom's electrons scatter. It is like a pool ball hitting a group of pool balls. Certain elements are unstable. They release particles to increase stability. They release energy to increase stability. This release is called radioactivity. This happens because too many particles exist in the atom. The atom cannot be stable with too many particles. Think of a crowded elevator. Many people are inside. Everyone feels uncomfortable. Some people will leave the group. They do not stick together. They do not go all the way to the top. Eventually enough people leave. The elevator becomes comfortable again. This is how lead forms. Lead is uranium that has released enough particles. It becomes stable. It becomes comfortable enough. The particles stay together. They do not lose anyone. Radiation means different types of light. Radio waves are one type. X-rays are another type. Other types exist beyond these. Some atoms are radioactive. Radioactive atoms fall apart. Energetic bits fly off when they fall apart. Gamma rays are one kind of bit. Gamma rays are a form of light. Gamma rays are therefore radiation. Scientists first discovered radioactivity long ago. They did not fully understand the different kinds of light then. Much confusion existed. People confused what was radiation. People confused what was radioactivity. People confused what was both. Some people still use radiation when they mean radioactivity. Here is a review. Radiation means different kinds of light. Radioactivity means bits that fly off radioactive atoms. Gamma rays are both radiation and radioactivity.
style_simplified.coling::3dd39352-d471-4ab9-bd50-b7345fc1: You can call this thing a wealth tax. You can also call it a capital tax. These taxes work in a different way than income taxes. Income taxes are based on money you earned in one year. Wealth taxes are based on how much you own. Different countries use different kinds of wealth taxes. Italy taxes people who own land in foreign countries. I believe Italy is a good example of this. Some countries tax the amounts that corporations own. Canada did this until about five to ten years ago. The exact time depended on which province you lived in. Some countries tax your wealth if it goes above a certain level. Switzerland does this. People have mentioned Switzerland already. The United States has one form of this tax. It is called the Estate Tax. This tax is based on how much wealth a person owns. The tax happens when they die. The threshold for this tax has changed a lot. It has changed over the last twenty years. The threshold is generally in the multi-millions. I believe it sits somewhere around five million dollars right now. These taxes might start to appear more and more. I believe they will. Do not be shocked at the initial price tag. A wealth tax could replace some of the current income tax in many countries. It could do this without creating a strict increased tax burden. Here is an example. You owe ten thousand dollars in income tax this year. A two thousand dollar capital tax starts next year. Your income tax is reduced to eight thousand dollars. You are still in the same position. Whether these taxes work well is a question of economics. It is not a question of personal finance. I will not discuss that point further. One more note. Your saved money might earn money. It might earn interest or dividends or rent from a condo you own. Those earnings are typically taxed alongside your wage income. Any wealth tax or capital tax would be in addition to income tax on investment earnings.
style_simplified.coling::8eb96c1a-6193-4f0f-843b-4b91efbe: You could have both options exercised on the same day. Both could be assigned to you on the same day. But I don't think you could lose money on both on the same day. Here is the reason. Exercises happen right away. Assignments are processed later. They are processed after the markets close. This happens at the end of each day. You can see details at a website about options. You would get both assignments at the same time. This would happen that night. The net effect should be clear. You would not own any stock. Someone would put the stock to you. Then it would be called away. You would not have the options anymore. You should have cash coming in. This would be fifteen hundred dollars. You get this from selling the stock to the call exerciser. You should have cash going out. This would be thirteen hundred dollars. You pay this to buy from the put exerciser. Is that right? You would have no more options. But you would have two hundred dollars more cash in your account. This would show up in the morning. You bought at thirteen. You sold at fifteen. This options position is an agreement. You agree to buy at thirteen. You agree to sell at fifteen. This happens at someone else's option. The way you lose money is different. One of the options is not exercised. But the other one is exercised. The stock might be below thirteen. Nobody is going to choose to buy from you at fifteen. But they will sell to you at thirteen. Or the stock might be above fifteen. Nobody is going to choose to sell to you at thirteen. But they will buy from you at fifteen. You make money in two situations. Neither option is exercised. You keep the premium you sold for. Or both are exercised. You keep the gap between the two prices. You also keep the premium. Having both exercised is surely rare. Early exercise is rare to begin with. It tends to happen when options are deep in the money. You would expect both to be exercised if both are deep in the money at some point. Having both be exercised on the same day cannot be common. But it is maybe most likely just before expiration. This happens with minimal time value. The stock moves around quickly. Both options are in the money at some point during the day.

You need to do something first. You need to look at your credit card terms and conditions. Or you can ask your bank a question. You need to know how they apply your payments. One person named Dilip wrote an answer. He talked about the US. In the US, banks will likely do something specific. They apply the minimum payment to the lower rate balance. Then they must apply the rest to the higher rate balance. The rest means anything above the minimum. In other countries, things work differently. Laws are different. Customs are different. Do not assume anything. Do not assume the bank will pay off the higher balance first. Do not assume they will pay proportionally. You must ask them.

Let's look at an example. You owe a total of six thousand dollars. Five thousand dollars is at one rate. That rate is thirteen point five percent. This is the normal purchase rate. One thousand dollars is at a different rate. That rate is twenty two percent. This is the cash advance rate. Your bank might apply payments to both balances proportionally. Then a payment of six hundred dollars will reduce your purchase balance by five hundred dollars. It will reduce your cash advance balance by one hundred dollars.

The average APR is simple to calculate. You multiply each APR times its balance. Then you add those products together. So here you do this calculation. You multiply point one three five times five thousand. You multiply point two two five times one thousand. You add those two numbers. You divide by six thousand. The answer is fifteen percent. This is called a weighted average.

The bank might apply the payment differently. They might apply it to the lower rate first. They might apply some specified part to the lower rate. They apply the rest to the higher rate. Then this calculation will be misleading. You might enter it into a calculator. But your average APR will rise over time. This happens as you pay off the purchase balance. You don't pay off the cash advance balance. Or it may decrease. This happens if the opposite occurs.

The weighted average is probably reasonably close. This works in the circumstance you describe. This works even if you have rules applying the balance differently. But they must not pay down the lower rate one hundred percent. So it may be the simplest option for you. This works for rough calculations. These are calculations where being correct is not critical. Being close is enough.

One approach might be better. You can use online calculators. You treat these like two separate loans. You treat them like two separate cards. Many calculators exist. They handle multiple balances. Then you can allocate funds differently to the two cards. This would let you see something. You can see how long you will need to pay off the higher balance. It probably will not perfectly match things. You would need to find a site. The site must have this specific option available. Otherwise you will have to live with a small error in your calculations. Or you do the math by hand.
style_simplified.coling::9e189795-5152-41d4-9713-20ef5189: Wyoming is a good state for this. It does not cost much money. You do not have to do much each year to stay in compliance. This person needs to go in person to a bank. They will open an account there. This person needs to be mentioned in the Operating Agreement. Or they need to be in another official form. style_simplified.coling::df393828-70be-448f-bbdb-11367e15:
I want to say this very clearly. I will say it more than once. Do not plan your money around your credit score. Do not think about your credit score at all. Make a budget. Follow that budget. Put savings in your budget. Save for things you need soon. Save for things you need later. Pay your bills when they are due. Use credit cards in a smart way. Do all of these things. Your credit rating will be good. It will take care of itself. Do not try to plan your money to make it go up.

Now I will talk about zero percent financing. This is when you can borrow money and pay no interest. I have a rule for this. I only use it when I have saved enough money to buy the thing with cash. I also check my budget first. The loan payment must fit in my budget. Other people have different rules. Some people never take these loans at all. You should make a rule that works for you. But you should have a rule. One rule you should not have is this. Do not do things just to make your credit score better. You should not plan your money around your credit score.

Here is the most important thing for you right now. Do not let the low rate trick you. It might make you buy things you would not normally buy. You are not getting free money. style_news_dates_suffixes.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of temporal behavior patterns in complex systems represents a key requirement across numerous scientific fields during the 2020s. style_news_dates_suffixes.coling::7876816d-0ac2-4404-b2bf-deeaa0b7: The CII 158 micron line represents the most significant coolant of the interstellar medium in galaxies, but substantial variations in its emission are observed from object to object. Previous investigations of CII emission in galaxies have achieved resolutions of several kiloparsecs or more, resulting in the observation of averaged emission from different ISM components. The aim of this investigation is the examination, for the first time, of CII emission at the scale of a spiral arm. The investigation of the origin of this line and its utilization as a tracer of star formation activity constitutes the primary objective. This presentation includes CII and OI observations of a segment of a spiral arm of Messier 31 obtained using the Infrared Space Observatory during the 1995-1998 operational period. The CII emission undergoes comparison with tracers of neutral gas including carbon monoxide and neutral hydrogen and indicators of star formation activity including H-alpha and Spitzer Space Telescope 24 micron observations from 2003-2009. The similarity of the CII emission distribution with the H-alpha and 24 micron images proves striking when smoothing to identical resolution occurs, whereas the correlation with neutral gas distributions demonstrates much weaker correspondence. The CII cooling rate per hydrogen atom increases dramatically from approximately 2.7 times 10 to the minus 26 ergs per second per atom in the border regions of the mapped area to approximately 1.4 times 10 to the minus 25 ergs per second per atom in the regions of active star formation. The CII to FIR (42-122 micron) ratio maintains near constancy at 2 percent, representing a factor of 3 elevation above typically quoted values. However, the interpretation suggests that Messier 31 does not constitute an unusual case. So, you know, being able to predict how complex systems behave over time, right, that's really crucial in so many scientific fields. But, well, there's this huge problem that gets in the way.

Oh yeah? What's that?

Well, I mean, often we just don't have access to the equations that describe the physics of whatever system we're looking at. Or, you know, even if we do know them, hmm, solving them might take way too long—like, the computation time just doesn't work with how fast we need predictions.

Right, right. So what do people do about that?

Well, it's become pretty common now—especially with machine learning, you know—to just approximate these complex systems using some generic functional format and train it from scratch using whatever observations we have available. I mean, deep neural networks have shown tons of successful examples of this.

Sure, but there's got to be downsides, right?

Oh, absolutely. See, things like how well the models generalize, what guarantees we have, the impact of the data—these often get overlooked or, you know, they're only examined by relying on prior physics knowledge.

Hmm, so how do you tackle that?

Well, we approach it differently—we use this curriculum learning strategy. So basically, you structure the dataset so training starts with simple samples and gradually moves toward more complex ones. This helps with convergence and generalization. The concept's been developed and successfully applied in robotics and control already.

Okay, and how exactly do you apply it here?

Right, so first, we use insights from ergodic theory to figure out how much data is sufficient to guarantee a faithful model. We thoroughly investigate how the training set and its structure impact long-term predictions. Then we consider entropy as a complexity metric for the dataset. We show that designing the training set based on entropy analysis significantly improves generalizability and provides insights on the amount and choice of data needed for effective data-driven modeling.

So, um, you know that CII 158 microns line, right? Well, it's like the most important coolant of the interstellar medium in galaxies, but—

Oh yeah, I mean, the thing is there are substantial variations from object to object, you know?

Right, exactly. And well, the main source of the emission at a galactic scale is still poorly understood, which is—

Hmm, so previous studies of the CII emission in galaxies, they have a resolution of several kpc or more, right?

Yeah, so I mean the observed emission is basically an average of different ISM components. So anyway, the aim of this work is to study, for the first time, the CII emission at the scale of a spiral arm, you know?

Oh, so you want to investigate the origin of this line and its use as a tracer of star formation?

Exactly! So we present CII and OI observations of a segment of a spiral arm of M~31 using the Infrared Space Observatory. The CII emission is compared with tracers of neutral gas—CO, HI—and star formation, like H alpha and Spitzer 24 mu.

And well, the similarity of the CII emission with the Ha and 24 mu images is striking when smoothed to the same resolution, right? Whereas the correlation with the neutral gas is much weaker.

Right, I mean the CII cooling rate per H atom increases dramatically from about 2.7e-26 ergs per second per atom in the border of the map to like 1.4e-25 ergs per second per atom in the regions of star formation.

Oh, and the CII over FIR ratio, that 42 to 122, it's almost constant at 2 percent—

Which is a factor 3 higher than typically quoted! But we don't believe that M~31 is unusual though.

No, I mean, the whole-galaxy fluxes used for the comparisons include the central regions where the CII over FIR ratio is known to be lower, you know? And well, a fit to published PDR models yields a plausible average solution of G naught around 100 and n around 3000 for the PDR emission in the regions of star formation in the arm of M31.

So we're looking at this, um, two-dimensional tight-binding model, right? It's a topological crystalline insulator — you know, a TCI — and it's protected by rotation symmetry.

Oh, interesting. How'd you build it?

Well, we stacked two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers, and they transform under these conjugate representations of the rotation group. I mean, like p-plus and p-minus orbitals, you know?

Hmm, so it's kind of like the Kane-Mele model then?

Yeah, it looks similar, but here's the thing — it doesn't actually host stable gapless surface states.

Wait, really? But does it show any topological responses?

Oh yeah, definitely! We see quantized fractional charge that's bound to these rotational defects — disclinations, right? And there's this pumping of angular momentum when you thread an elementary magnetic flux through it. It's all described by this mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and, well, an effective gauge field for the rotation symmetry.

Okay, and what about Wannier representations?

Right, so the filled bands don't admit a symmetric Wannier representation. But — and this is important — when you add appropriate atomic orbitals, that obstruction goes away. So it's what we call fragile topology.

Which means?

I mean, you can represent the response as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients, you know?

Hmm. Does this apply more broadly?

Oh yes! So after analyzing this model as a prototypical example, we showed that all TCIs protected by point group symmetries without protected surface states are either atomic insulators or fragile phases. Remarkably, gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only if there's a stable Wannier obstruction.

And then?

Well, we used dimensional reduction to map the 2D problem to a zero-dimensional one, which gave us the complete non-interacting classification and how interactions reduce it.
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243:
So, um, we've got this new AI thing we're calling the Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate, right? DSNS for short. Basically, what it does is, well, it takes different features from objects in all sorts of areas, you know, like chess problems, classical music, famous paintings, that kind of stuff.

Yeah, and then it mixes them together to create new features that can be used to make, I mean, novel things that people might actually find creative and valuable in any of those original areas.

Right, so it's like passing some of the creative work from humans over to machines, you know?

Hmm, okay, so how did you test it?

Well, we tried it out with chess problem composition. We used it to automatically create tons of chess problems by taking attributes from chess problems and tournament games that humans played, and also from famous paintings, computer-generated abstract art, photos of people, and classical music pieces.

Oh, interesting! And how did you know if they were any good?

Well, we assessed the quality automatically using this existing chess aesthetics model that's been validated through experiments. But we also had human experts in chess look at them too.

Right, right. And what did you find?

The results show that, you know, attributes gathered and mixed from chess and other areas using DSNS can actually generate chess problems with pretty high aesthetic quality. Oh, and here's something really surprising—a low quality chess source, like tournament games between weak players, combined with actual photographs of people, produced three-move problems that were just as good or even better than ones from high quality sources, I mean published compositions by experts. And more efficiently too!

Hmm, that's weird. Why does information from a completely different domain even work like that?

Yeah, well, that's still an open question for now. But the approach should work, in principle, for any domain where objects have attributes you can represent with real numbers.

So, you know that baryon acoustic oscillation peak, right? The BAO thing we see in cosmic matter distribution out to, like, redshift 3.5 or so?

Yeah, yeah.

Well, it's basically showing us the continued expansion of that sonic horizon we first spotted in the cosmic microwave background temperature patterns.

Oh, interesting.

Right, and I mean, we can now measure where that BAO peak sits to better than 1% accuracy when we use galaxies, you know? With Ly-alpha forests and quasar clustering, we're getting about 1.4 to 1.6% precision.

Hmm, okay.

So anyway, when you combine this with the Alcock-Paczyński effect—

The AP effect, right?

Exactly. That's the one that comes from how the ratio of angular to spatial size changes with distance for these spherically-symmetric sources, you know?

Oh yeah, I see.

Well, the BAO measurement is considered one of the most powerful tools we have for assessing the Universe's geometry.

Makes sense.

So in this paper, we used five BAO peak measurements from the final Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV release. Average redshifts were 0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48, and 2.33.

Wow, okay.

And we did a direct head-to-head comparison between Lambda-CDM—the standard model—and one of its main competitors, the R_h=ct universe.

Hmm, interesting approach.

Right, so we also used a volume-averaged distance probe that assumes constant comoving distance scale r_d, you know, for completeness. Both probes don't depend on uncertain parameters like the Hubble constant, so they're ideal for model selection.

And what did you find?

Well, based solely on the AP effect, R_h=ct was favored with about 75% likelihood versus 25% for the standard model. But with the volume-averaged distance probe, Planck-Lambda-CDM was favored—about 80% versus 20%.

Oh wow.

Yeah, and the joint analysis? Inconclusive. Both models got comparable likelihoods. So we can't really confirm that BAO data alone support an accelerating Universe.

So, you know, filaments are basically everywhere in the Galaxy, right? And well, they're where stars form, so I mean, being able to detect them reliably is really key to understanding how star formation actually works.

Oh, okay, so what are you trying to do?

Well, we're exploring whether supervised machine learning can identify these filamentary structures across the whole Galactic plane.

Hmm, interesting. So how did you do it?

Right, so we used two versions of these UNet-based networks for image segmentation. I mean, we took H2 column density images of the Galactic plane—you know, obtained with Herschel Hi-GAL data—as our input. Then we trained the UNet networks with skeletons of filaments, like the spine plus branches, that we extracted from these images. Oh, and we also produced background and missing data masks. We tested eight different training scenarios to figure out the best one for classifying pixels as filaments.

And what did you find?

Well, the training lets us create this new image of the Galactic plane by segmentation where pixels belonging to filamentary structures are identified. With this new method, we actually classify way more pixels as belonging to filaments—I mean, more by a factor of two to seven, depending on the threshold we use—than the spine plus branches structures we started with. New structures are revealed too, which are mainly these low-contrast filaments that weren't detected before. We used standard metrics to evaluate the different training scenarios, right? This shows the method is robust and helps us determine an optimal threshold that maximizes recovery of the input labelled pixel classification.

So what's the takeaway?

Well, this proof-of-concept shows that supervised machine learning can reveal filamentary structures throughout the Galactic plane. Detecting these structures, including low-density and low-contrast ones never seen before, offers really important perspectives for studying these filaments.

"Okay, so, um, I have to be honest here — I'm actually undecided on this whole thing, right? But I'm gonna start by arguing against gay marriage for, well, two reasons basically. First, you know, I lean less towards that side and it seems way more fragile and unpopular, so like, advocating for the weaker position that I feel less strongly about? That helps me practice my argument skills, I mean, you know what I mean? And second, I think — and I'll explain this — the burden of proof is on the side that's for gay marriage, so that's why I started on the other side."

"Hmm, okay, go on."

"Right, so first, there's this video — it's only two minutes — and because of that argument, I feel like the burden of proof is on people who want to redefine what marriage means. I don't have a problem with redefinition itself, but, well, you need a compelling reason to redefine something, right?"

"Sure, yeah."

"So when people answer 'Do you think gay marriage is a good idea?' with 'Why not?' — that's really just the teapot fallacy, you know? They're trying to shift the burden of proof."

"Oh, I see what you're saying."

"And I don't think equality is a good argument here. I mean, it's true that people with different sexual orientations deserve equal rights to life, liberty, freedom, pursuit of happiness — all that stuff in the constitution. But the whole equality thing? It's a red herring in this case."

"Wait, how so?"

"Well, marriage isn't a privilege or a right that has to be equal for all types of relationships. Marriage is an institution built around procreation, right? And homosexual relationships, which can be loving and committed, by definition are non-procreational."

"But what about—"

"Yeah, yeah, I know — there are heterosexual marriages that are non-procreational too, like old couples or infertile couples. But if you watch that video, you'll understand why it's not the same thing. Just because there are exceptions to the norm doesn't mean you can extend the definition to a non-norm, because norms aren't defined by their exceptions, you know?"

"Hmm, okay."

"This 'equality' isn't the same as women voting or black people being free. And, oh, another thing — people present the criteria as 'If two people love each other, why shouldn't they be able to get married?' But marriage criteria have nothing to do with love, or even romantic love."

"Really?"

"Yeah! I mean, if your criteria are two individuals who have romantic or sexual love, then incest is fair game, right?"

"Oh, well, but incest is different because—"

"Because of power issues and genetic defects? Well, there can be power issues in any relationship — heterosexual, homosexual, or incestuous. There's no reason to base marriage legislation on that. And incestuous couples don't have to have children, they can adopt, or they might be infertile or even homosexual themselves."

"So you're saying—"

"Someone could argue that incest should be a valid form of marriage just like homosexuality. You can try to argue against that if you want, but you need valid reasoning because the burden of proof is on you."

"Okay, but—"

"And the 'why would you care?' argument? That's invalid. Just because something doesn't affect anyone badly doesn't mean we can change institutions at whim. Even under utilitarianism, this doesn't work. Gay people can have fulfilling long-term romantic and sexual relationships without calling it marriage, right? Redefining marriage for one group's happiness is like — logically, not emotionally — giving in to lobbyist demands so they'll be happier."

"Hmm."

"Most arguments for gay marriage are appeals to emotion or popularity. The term 'gay rights' was designed to make it sound like we have internment camps for them! Even 'homophobe' was coined to stigmatize the opposition. Just because this issue is popular now, and many opponents are religious fundamentalists using straw man arguments, doesn't make the 'more reasonable side' correct. I mean, if there was a movement to legalize incestuous marriage and it was popular, with videos and websites glorifying those couples, most people would support that too. Why is one sexual deviation — and I mean that with complete respect, no stigma at all — more 'marriageable' than another?"

"Well, you know what? My view actually changed. To be fair though, I was already like seventy-five percent there when I started this whole thing."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::bd4df89c-701f-407b-9fc6-2c51aa5b:
So like, I'm talking about this kind of condemnation that you hear all the time from, you know, certain users on rpolitics, right, and certain OWS members, and oh, that Gawker writer Hamilton Nolan, you know? It's basically this viewpoint, and I mean, I'll paraphrase it roughly here, but it goes something like: the mere fact that we live in a system where some people can amass vastly more money than others is, well, it's immoral in itself, right? And if you do amass wealth under this system, hmm, you're quite arguably a bad person, you know?

Yeah, exactly. Like, hedge fund managers are sitting around spending tens of millions on embalmed sharks and—

Right, right, and don't they know that a tiny fraction of their daily earnings would make a huge difference in other people's lives? I mean, it would be enough to pay off the average redditor's student loans, for example.

Oh totally. Every time I've heard this shitty argument though, I've heard it from activists or internet commenters who hail from, well, the middle-class tier, or maybe working-class tier, of an advanced Western economy.

Hmm, okay, but here's the thing though—

You too have vastly more resources than most people worldwide, right?

Well, yeah, I mean—

Like, if you could save a hundred bucks by not upgrading your smartphone, or by walking home in the rain instead of taking a cab, or eating lentils or beans for a few weeks, or by foregoing that new item of clothing you wanted, you know, you could donate that hundred dollars to save the lives of dozens of kids who would otherwise die of malaria.

Right, so is your comfort, your convenience and entertainment more important than other people's lives?

I mean—

And btw, I will not tolerate deflections to the effect of, oh, "but charities might not use the money responsibly," or "charitable donations could have negative effects on local industry in the long run." You know? As a premise of this CMV, we must stipulate that if wealth could be redistributed, that redistribution would, indeed, benefit the recipients, okay? We must further stipulate that if the average American wanted to donate in a genuinely beneficial manner towards a worthy cause, well, he'd be able to do so. I don't think these are crazy assumptions to make, right?

Yeah, so your view is—

So my view is that people who rail against "the rich," purely on the ground that they're rich, are hypocrites for overlooking their own relative economic standing in the world. If they believe others' wealth should be redistributed to curb inequality, they are hypocrites for not redistributing their own wealth to curb inequality, you know?

Hmm, okay.

Now, I don't donate much to charity, but nor do I regard people richer than me as innately evil human beings. I can acknowledge the preference revealed by my decision-making, which is: I'd rather upgrade to business class than save five hundred lives in a developing country, right? For this reason, if some billionaire would rather upgrade his yacht than dissolve all his assets to promote communism, well, I don't really blame him.

Right, but it seems quite a few people disagree with you?

Yeah, exactly, so I'm curious to see if anyone can change my view here, you know?
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::4b504a77-e4f6-447f-996a-b39d54b5:
Hey, did you hear what happened with those Houthi rebels in Yemen?

Oh yeah, I mean, their leader came out on Sunday and basically said they're not backing down, right?

Right, right. What was his name again? Abdul-Malik al-Houthi?

Yeah, that's him. So anyway, he gave this televised address and was like, you know, our fighters aren't leaving the main cities or government buildings.

Hmm, so he's pretty defiant then?

Oh totally! He even said, well, anyone who thinks we'll surrender is dreaming. I mean, those were his actual words.

Wow. But wait, didn't the Saudis say something different?

Oh yeah, yeah. So there's this top Saudi military official who's claiming the airstrikes have really weakened them significantly.

Right, and those airstrikes have been going on for weeks now, haven't they?

Yeah, more than three weeks actually. The Saudi-led coalition has been bombing them trying to push them back. I mean, the Houthis surged into the capital back in January, right? Sanaa?

Oh right, and they ousted that president. What's his name... Hadi?

Yeah, Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi. Well, he still claims he's the legitimate leader and he's working with the Saudis to get back.

Hmm, so how bad has it gotten?

Well, since mid-March, more than seven hundred people have been killed. I mean, the violence just shows no sign of slowing down.

Oh my god, that's terrible. So what else did al-Houthi say?

He said, you know, the Yemeni people have the right to stand against the attacks by all possible means. And he said something about not wanting to hear any voices or cries after people react to children and women being killed.

Right, right. But wait, aren't there some cracks forming?

Oh yeah! So there's this general, AbdulRahman AlHalili, who leads like ten thousand troops. He used to be loyal to the former president but now he's allied with Hadi.

Interesting. What about the Saudi side?

Well, their brigadier general, Asiri, said Sunday the airstrikes have decimated the Houthis' central command. They've launched twenty-three hundred airstrikes since late March.

Wow, that's intense.
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::ef2146c2-c9fe-4563-b26a-b39f1bb9:
"Oh my God, so you heard about that mom with six boys, right?"

"Wait, which one?"

"The one from Apex, North Carolina. Cher Lair. She just found out she's having a girl!"

"No way! After how many tries?"

"Seven! This is baby number seven. I mean, can you imagine?"

"Wow, okay, so how'd she find out?"

"Well, so she had this gender reveal party, you know, with all the family around and everything."

"Oh right, with the cake?"

"Exactly! So she didn't know what she was having, right? She gave the scan results to a baker."

"Smart, yeah."

"And when she cut into it and lifted up the slice, it was pink! Pink sponge cake!"

"Oh man, I bet she just—"

"Dude, she screamed so loud! Like, the video says it was deafening. She literally fell backwards."

"Are you serious?"

"Yes! And then she got down on her knees and just kept saying 'Oh my God, oh my God' over and over, like panting."

"I mean, after six boys though, right?"

"Right! Everyone around her was cheering and clapping. You could hear them in the background."

"So wait, had they given up on having a girl?"

"Yeah! She told the TV station, um, WTVD, that she and her husband Stephen had totally given up."

"Hmm, I get that."

"She said, you know, with baby three and four she was thinking there'd be a girl at some point. Like, they can't all be boys."

"Makes sense."

"But then after four and five and six, she was like, 'Yeah, they can.' All boys."

"Oh wow. So when did she find out?"

"Monday. A friend knew the sex and baked the chocolate cake, made it pink inside."

"That's so sweet."

"Yeah. But now she's nervous, you know, about a girl coming into such a boy house."

"Well sure, yeah."

"But she's excited too! She wants to do all the mommy-daughter things. Take her to see Cinderella, get pedicures and manicures, shop for prom dresses."

"Aww, that's really nice."

"I know! And get this—the video's been watched over a hundred thousand times already."

"Seriously?"

"Yeah! People are loving it. One person commented that the little girl's gonna be so lucky having six big brothers to look after her."

"Oh, that's true. She'll be protected forever."

"Right? So she's due in August."

"Do they have names picked out yet?"

"Hmm, no word on that yet. Nothing announced anyway."

"Well, I'm sure they'll figure it out. That's just amazing though."

"I know, right?"
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::a1534ce8-2639-4c7c-b509-3d430b55:
"Hey, did you hear about Migos getting arrested?"

"Oh man, no! What happened?"

"Well, so they were on tour, right? First leg of their U.S. tour, and they got busted at this college show."

"Seriously? Where was this?"

"Georgia Southern University. So like, the cops found drugs and guns in their van during the gig."

"Wait, during the actual performance?"

"Yeah! So there's Quavious Marshall, he's 24, um, Kirschnick Ball who's 20, and Kiari Cephus, 23, right? They got escorted off campus mid-performance on Saturday night."

"Oh wow, that's crazy. Mid-performance?"

"Yeah, I mean, they literally took them off stage and into custody."

"Hmm, so what's happening with their tour then?"

"Well, that's the thing. NBC News said all of them got denied bond, you know? So they might not be able to do their upcoming shows at all."

"Right, right. Where were they supposed to go next?"

"Let's see, um, they had this Ksu Convocation Center show in Georgia, and then they were traveling to like Wisconsin, Ohio, Michigan, Pennsylvania, New York — a bunch of states."

"So how'd the cops even know to search them?"

"Oh, okay, so authorities said there was this really potent smell of marijuana coming from their two tour buses."

"Ah, I see."

"Yeah, and when Migos left to perform at the Hanner Fieldhouse arena, investigators were like, perfect opportunity, you know? So they searched the buses."

"What'd they find?"

"Multiple guns, marijuana, and some other drug they didn't say what it was."

"Geez."

"I mean, officials said the discoveries were intensely concerning because, well, it's a university-sponsored event with over a thousand students there."

"Right, that makes sense. So what are they being charged with?"

"Um, drug possession, possession of firearms in a school safety zone, and possession of firearms during commission of a crime."

"That's serious stuff. Do they have lawyers?"

"Wasn't known on Monday if they had attorneys yet. The Associated Press tried calling and emailing their management team but didn't hear back."

"Were they the only ones arrested?"

"No! About a dozen other people got taken into custody too — all occupants from the two vans."

"Oh wow."

"Yeah, but there's no information yet about what charges those people face."

"Hmm. Weren't Migos pretty big? I mean, they had some hits, right?"

"Oh yeah! They're best known for Versace from 2013 and Fight Night from 2014. They formed back in 2009."

"And this was during what, some special concert?"

"Yeah, the school's annual spring concert. Migos had actually contracted with Georgia Southern to perform there."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::49a2d576-81e8-4b16-889d-beb4a986:
"Oh man, did you hear about that teenager in the Bronx?"

"Hmm, no, what happened?"

"Well, so this seventeen-year-old kid, Hakeem Kuta, right, he died after falling off a roof. Six stories."

"What? Oh my god, that's terrible!"

"Yeah, I know. So basically what happened was, um, police were responding to complaints about some kids smoking weed and hanging around in a building lobby, you know?"

"Right, okay."

"So Hakeem and like five other teenagers, they ran when the cops showed up. I mean, they just bolted up the stairs to the roof."

"Oh jeez."

"Yeah, and the thing is, he was a junior at Bronx Envision Academy. Anyway, so the cops chased them up there, right? And when the officers got to the roof, well, some of the teens jumped over to another roof and got away."

"Uh huh."

"But Hakeem and this fourteen-year-old kid with him, they got trapped by this dividing wall, you know? They were pinned in."

"Oh no."

"So then, I mean, Hakeem jumped over this three-foot wall, but here's the thing—he didn't realize there was this gap between the buildings."

"Oh god, really?"

"Yeah, yeah. And his friend, the fourteen-year-old, he tried to help him. He was holding onto Hakeem's jacket, desperately trying to keep him from falling. The kid was dangling like sixty feet above an alleyway."

"Jesus, that's—"

"I know, right? And then this officer, um, Edmundo Rivera, he grabbed onto the friend to stop him from going over the edge too. But the friend, he lost his grip on Hakeem and, well, he fell. Six stories down to the pavement."

"Oh my god, that's horrible."

"Yeah, so the police ran down to where he fell in the courtyard, and they took him to St. Barnabas Hospital. He was in critical condition on life support."

"Did he—"

"He died Saturday morning, around eleven. This happened Thursday night, so yeah."

"That's so sad. I mean, was he in trouble or something?"

"Well, that's the thing. His father, Munir—he's forty-two, immigrant from Ghana—he said his son stayed out of trouble, doesn't do drugs."

"Really?"

"Yeah, he said, you know, 'It's not so easy. He was a nice kid.'"

"Hmm."

"And get this—the authorities said there probably wouldn't have been any arrests anyway. They just wanted the kids to stop smoking marijuana."

"Seriously?"

"Yeah, I mean, no summonses were issued. They did recover marijuana in the lobby, but still."

"So he died running from something that wasn't even—"

"Exactly. Just trying to get them to leave, you know? The building was on Valentine Avenue in Mott Haven."

"Man, that's just tragic. Over nothing, really."

"I know, right? Seventeen years old. His whole life ahead of him."

"Yeah. God, that's awful."

"It really is."

style_dialogue_interjections.coling::6d5e183d-832b-4aa4-a6e2-563f2423:
"Oh man, did you hear about that Chinese policewoman who fought off some guy with a machete?"

"Wait, what? With her bare hands?"

"Yeah, I mean, she was completely unarmed! Her name's Cao Yu, she's only 22 years old, you know?"

"That's insane. Where did this happen?"

"Well, it was in Guizhou province, right, in southwestern China. Happened earlier this month in some public square."

"So what exactly went down?"

"Okay, so she was on patrol, right, and she sees this guy in his twenties waving around a machete. Actually, he had two knives."

"Oh my god."

"I know! So she confronts him, and he stabs her in the shoulder. The whole thing lasted like five minutes."

"Five minutes? That's forever when someone's attacking you!"

"Right? And get this — the machete was 60 centimeters long. Huge knife. She kept fighting him off even after getting stabbed, and she got more wounds on both her hands before her colleagues finally showed up."

"Jesus. Is she okay?"

"Well, she's in the hospital recovering now. They found her bleeding all over, you know. But she said something pretty amazing."

"What'd she say?"

"She said, 'I couldn't just let the man hurt innocent people.' Can you believe that?"

"Wow. That's incredible."

"Yeah, and she told the local TV station, I mean, she was trying to take the machete from him and stall him until backup arrived. She said there were lots of tourists walking around the square and she needed to make sure they were safe."

"So what was this guy doing anyway?"

"Apparently he'd robbed someone, and that's when Ms Cao spotted him."

"Hmm. What happened when the other cops got there?"

"Well, one of them, this guy Jiao Chun, he said they told the guy to drop the machete but he wouldn't. He kept saying he wanted to rob someone for more money."

"That's messed up."

"Oh, and the story got even bigger when CCTV footage came out this week. Chinese social media went crazy for her."

"I bet!"

"Yeah, on Weibo — you know, their version of Twitter — people were calling her a real tough girl. One person posted something like, 'Those who say they're tough every day aren't tough at all!'"

"Ha! That's true though."

"But someone else asked a good question, actually. They were like, 'Where are the qualified policemen? Why didn't they send an armed, well-trained officer to deal with this guy?'"

"Right, that does seem weird. Why send an unarmed young woman?"

"Exactly. Makes you wonder if they're just too shorthanded or what."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::23d0bd02-f2a0-4752-971c-cac75280:
Person1: Hey Rocky! You know, you've been sitting around all night, man. I mean, get out there and dance with someone, like, oh, that woman over there.

Person2: No way! She looks like the intellectual type, you know?

Person1: Oh come on! What kind of woman do you like anyway?

Person2: Well, I want a woman who's affectionate and, you know, fulfills my every need, right? And that woman over there is just not the right type for me.

Person1: Hey, wait. Where have you been? I mean, times are changing, and you're never going to find a woman who'll shine your shoes and pick up after you all the time, man. Wake up already.

Person2: Oh really? Well, I meet a lot of women like that, but, you know, not at this party. Oh, and I also prefer a woman who'll stay home, cook, clean, and watch the kids, right?

Person1: Okay, but what are your household responsibilities once you get home from work, hmm?

Person2: Hmm. Well, eat, watch TV, and throw out the garbage.

Person1: Wait, wait, wait. I can't believe I'm hearing this, man. In fact, you're never going to get married, you know? I recently read a news report that said 40 percent of women don't think their husbands do their share around the house, and you seem to be that type, right?

Person2: Well, that's the way I am, but what's YOUR idea of the perfect woman then?

Person1: Well, I like a woman who's outgoing, caring, and non-judgmental about people's differences, you know? And it bothers me when people think they're the center of the universe, I mean, like someone I know.

Person2: Well, that's nice for you, but that doesn't change my point of view. I guess I'll have to go home to a TV dinner and my dog, Rusty.

Person1: Hey, and if I stick with you, this is going to be a long, lonely night, man. Say hello to Rusty for me.
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::65648d18-be4d-475d-bcab-2fbcdb8a:
"Hey, so like, there's really two different questions here, you know?"

"Oh yeah? What do you mean?"

"Well, okay, so first the bridge thing. I mean, the Atlantic is really really big, right? Like depending on where you cross it could be even bigger than the whole USA."

"Wow, okay."

"And on top of that, um, it's wet obviously and it gets these crazy storms which can cause quite a bit of damage to concrete and steel, you know, the stuff you'd use to make the bridge."

"Right, right."

"So the ocean is too deep to sink the pilings down to anchor the bridge properly. And it's too stormy and full of waves so a pontoon type bridge would just shake itself to pieces."

"Hmm, makes sense."

"Oh, and it's also big and empty and very few people would really want to drive across it because, I mean, it would be so boring and they wouldn't be able to carry enough fuel for the whole trip anyway."

"Yeah, I guess—"

"I mean the adult version is we can't sink piling to stabilize the bridge and current structural materials won't stand up to the stresses of a pontoon bridge. Maintenance would be an absolute nightmare due to the corrosion from salt water and air. You could only refuel on the crossing if fuel were shipped out to the middle of the ocean, which basically defeats the purpose, right?"

"Oh wow, yeah. What about a tunnel then?"

"Well, okay, so the Atlantic is very very deep. All of that water on top of the ocean floor means there's lots of pressure at the bottom. Kind of like how your ears hurt when you dive deeply at the pool but multiply it by ten thousand."

"Ouch."

"Right? So all of that pressure means if they tried to dig a tunnel it would have to absolutely never ever spring a leak or the walls would crumble down and everyone would drown."

"That's terrifying."

"Oh, and on top of that you'd need really really big fans to make sure there was enough air for everyone down there. You would also have the same problem with fuel."

"Hmm."

"I mean, the real problem would be at the joins of the pre-fabricated tunnel sections which would go into the tunnel hole. There's no way they'd be able to be made strong enough to withstand the pressure and even small leaks at that pressure would penetrate materials like a movie laser."

"Oh geez."

"And on top of that, ventilation of the tunnel would be an enormous issue. You would have thousands of kilometers of dead air that would have to be circulated somehow or you'd never make it through. As above, fuel as well."

"So basically nope?"

"Nope. The ocean is too vast, too deep, and too rough."

"Wait, I found something here online. Is the tunnel possible? Maybe?"

"Well, I guess you could call it just as possible as early nineteenth century engineers thought space travel was, you know?"

"Oh, I see."

"In other words, if enough scientists and politicians get hellbent on making this, it'll be made. Otherwise, very much doubt it."

"Right. Hey, ask yourself these questions though. Why would anyone want to drive all the way across the Atlantic?"

"Yeah, what benefit would a bridge or tunnel even have?"

"Exactly. Who would pay for the construction and how would they get a return on their investment? Who would also be responsible for maintaining it?"

"Hmm, good point."

"Remember this would be in international waters so what country or municipality would be responsible for the utilities and infrastructure?"

"Oh wow, yeah."

"Not feasible, not practical, not necessary."

"Oh, I haven't seen anyone else point this out but you would need to deal with the Mid Atlantic Ridge."

"What's that?"

"Well, the Atlantic Ocean is pulling itself apart at a rate of two point five centimeters a year. So you'll need to deal with volcanoes and earthquakes."

"Oh man."

"Even if someone manages to build a tunnel, would it be practical? Think about how far your car can travel before filling up or how many hours can you drive before getting too tired. If something happens in the middle of the tunnel, it would be hours before emergency personnel reaches there."

"True."

"I mean, absolutely it is possible, even with present technology. It's nowhere near economically viable however, since the cost would be absurdly high and the benefit minimal. The project becomes much more feasible with the technological developments foreseen over the coming decades though."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::6ea6d618-d59e-455d-a265-490e1418:
"Hey, so you know how programs crash sometimes? Well, there are like, oh, so many reasons why that happens. Let me tell you about some of the common ones, okay?"

"Yeah, sure, go ahead."

"Alright, so first there's division by zero. You remember from, I mean, way back in kindergarten math, right? You can't divide a number by zero?"

"Oh right, yeah."

"Well, the result is undefined. So if a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer's gonna tell the program, hey, you're doing something wrong here. And if the program can't handle that situation, well, it may just crash."

"Hmm, okay, makes sense."

"Then there's access violation. So basically, a program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory, you know? Other parts are like, off-limits."

"Right, right."

"So if a program tries to access part of memory that's off-limits, the computer will tell the program that it's doing something wrong. And again, if the program can't handle that situation, it may crash."

"Got it."

"Oh, and then there's deadlock. Let me explain this one. So let's say you and your friend Billy are playing with blocks, okay? You have the red block, and Billy has the blue block."

"Okay..."

"You want to switch blocks, so you tell Billy that you'll give him the red block after he gives you the blue block. But Billy tells you that he'll give you the blue block after you give him the red block."

"Oh no, I see where this is going."

"Yeah! Both of you will just sit there forever waiting for the other person to hand over their block, and you'll never get anything done. That's a deadlock situation, and when it happens inside a program, well, the program freezes up and there's nothing you can do except kill it and start it again."

"Wow, that's frustrating."

"I know, right? And then there's unhandled exception. Sometimes a program will have this special sort of error checking built into it, you know?"

"Uh-huh."

"When an error is detected, part of the program throws an exception, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with it. But if an exception gets thrown and is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a dialog will pop up letting you know that, hmm, a problem was not dealt with properly, and the program will terminate."

"Right, I've seen those pop-ups."

"Yeah! So all of these situations are caused by bugs in the program. Bugs are just parts of the program that aren't written correctly, or don't account for every possible thing that can happen."

"Makes sense. But why do some programs have more bugs than others?"

"Well, maybe because the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test it as well as they should have, you know? Or because the program is so complicated that it's difficult to deal with every possible situation that might happen."

"Oh, I get it now."

"Yeah, it's like, the more complex something is, the more things can go wrong with it, right?"

"Exactly, yeah."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::37e384a6-d2b8-444e-ac7f-d4288c17:
"So, you know, sometimes if there aren't that many athletes to fill up a whole race in one category, well, they'll run similar categories together. I mean, the less affected cerebral palsy athletes can ride with the less affected amputee riders, right, but they're only scored in their own class. Oh, they do this at most bike races for, you know, speeding things up and consolidating things."

"Right, right. So the Paralympics have a somewhat complicated system, hmm, of classifications and adjustments to try to keep things as fair as possible, you know?"

"Yeah, but unfortunately there aren't a lot of disabled athletes, and well, there's a wide variety of disabilities that confer different advantages and disadvantages."

"Oh, like what do you mean?"

"Well, for example, in wheelchair sports, amputees often have an advantage over those who are merely paralyzed because, you know, they're lighter and more maneuverable."

"Hmm, I see."

"So in the interest of having enough people to hold a competition, I mean, sometimes they just have to accept some disability types will have an advantage. This isn't really any different than the regular Olympics, right? Like, tall people have an advantage in basketball and no one's trying to fix that."

"Right, that makes sense. So how do they decide the categories?"

"Oh, well, the categories are based on what the disability causes, not necessarily the type of disability. If you look at cycling, the categories are people with upper body disabilities, people with one limb disability that can pedal with both legs, people with a leg injury where they only pedal with one leg, and people with both legs affected."

"So if CP affects the legs—"

"Yeah, they'd be put in the last category, just like someone else with another disability that affects both legs. Oh, and the athletes must be internationally classified, which requires an examination of how the disability affects the athlete. This helps ensure people can't game the system."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::5895f991-9d37-49fe-9f39-eeff324a:
"So yeah, they don't always just, you know, play dead. I mean, they also secrete these foul smelling liquids that, like, suggest the meat inside has already decayed, right?"

"Oh really?"

"Yeah! So not all predators can actually eat decayed meat, you know, so it gets left alone as the predator searches for safer food to eat."

"Hmm, that makes sense."

"Well, they also lack theory of mind, so it doesn't occur to them that something could be trying to trick them."

"Right, right."

"I would assume that an animal that even gives off the slightest signal of being sick will be avoided by predators, you know, as this could in turn sicken and potentially be the demise of the predator."

"Oh for sure."

"The animal playing dead may seem like a trivial display, but the predator has to weigh up the risks of possibly ingesting bacteria, viruses, whatever."

"Yeah, I mean, imagine you were defending yourself against someone and your adrenaline got all pumped up and you went batshit crazy at it to defend yourself, right?"

"Uh huh."

"At the point when they stop moving, well, the crisis is over and you start to feel safe again. Whether that is because they are unconscious, dead, or faking it, doesn't matter."

"Right."

"And you are a thinking, reasoning human being, not an animal acting solely on instinct, you know?"

"Oh yeah, exactly."

"Animals that are prey species will have instincts to protect themselves from being attacked and this includes trampling, headbutting, biting, goring with horns or antlers, whatever."

"Mmm hmm."

"Once the thing stops moving, the instinct to defend itself abates and it loses interest."

"Makes sense."

"Animals that hunt have similar instincts about prey that is running away or moving around, it triggers aggression. When the prey stops moving, it loses interest other than the need to feed if it's hungry."

"Right, so for something like a bear—"

"Exactly! Which will likely display territorial or defensive aggression and lose interest when the crisis is over. But this won't work on something like a pack of wolves, that are likely wanting to eat you."

"Oh god."

"Yeah, when you stop struggling, well, it's time to eat."
